### 11.2 Models for Predicting Human Performance Reliability and Correctability Probability in Transportation Systems

People involved with transportation systems perform various types of time continuous tasks including tracking, operating, and monitoring. In performing such tasks humans can make mistakes or errors and sometime can correct the self-generatederrors as well. Therefore, this section presents two mathematical models to predict human performance reliability and correctability probability.

# 11.2.1 Model I 

This model is concerned with predicting the human performance reliability or more specifically, the probability of performing a time continuous task correctly. An expression for predicting human performance reliability is developed as follows $[1-5]$.

The probability of occurrence of human error, say, in a transportation systemrelated task, in the finite time interval $\Delta t$ with event $Y$ given is

$$
P(X / Y)=\gamma(T) \Delta T
$$

where
$\gamma(t)$ is the human error rate at time $t$; this is analogous to the hazard rate, $z(t)$, in the classical reliability theory.
$X$ is an event that human error will occur in time interval $[t, t+\Delta t]$.
$Y$ is an errorless performance event of duration $t$.
The joint probability of the errorless performance is expressed by

$$
P(\bar{X} / Y) P(Y)=P(Y)-P(X / Y) P(Y)
$$

where
$\bar{X} \quad$ is the event that human error will not occur in time interval $[t, t+\Delta t]$.
$P(Y)$ is the occurrence probability of event $Y$.
It is to be noted that Equation (11.2) denotes an errorless performance probability over time intervals $[0, t]$ and $[t, t+\Delta t]$. Equation (11.2) may be rewritten as follows:

$$
R_{\mathrm{h}}(t)-R_{\mathrm{h}}(t) P(X / Y)=R_{\mathrm{h}}(t+\Delta t)
$$

where
$R_{\mathrm{h}}(t)$ is the human reliability at time $t$.
Substituting Equation (11.1) into Equation (11.3) yields

$$
\frac{R_{\mathrm{h}}(t+\Delta t)-R_{\mathrm{h}}(t)}{\Delta t}=-R_{\mathrm{h}}(t) \gamma(t)
$$

In the limiting case Equation (11.4) becomes

$$
\lim _{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} \frac{R_{\mathrm{h}}(t+\Delta t)-R_{\mathrm{h}}(t)}{\Delta t}=\frac{\mathrm{d} R_{\mathrm{h}}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=-R_{\mathrm{h}}(t) \gamma(t)
$$

At time $\mathrm{t}=0, R_{\mathrm{h}}(0)=1$.By rearranging the two right-hand terms of Equation (11.5), integrating the both sides over the time interval $[0, t]$, and using the above initial conditions, we get

$$
\int_{1}^{R_{\mathrm{h}}(t)} \frac{1}{R_{\mathrm{h}}(t)} \cdot \mathrm{d} R_{\mathrm{h}}(t)=-\int_{0}^{t} \gamma(t) \mathrm{d} t
$$

After evaluating the left side of Equation (11.6), we get

$$
R_{\mathrm{h}}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{1}{2} \gamma(t) \mathrm{d} t}
$$

The above equation is the general expression to compute human performance reliability for any time to human error statistical distribution (e.g., exponential, gamma, and Weibull).

By integrating Equation (11.7) over the time interval $[0, \infty]$, we obtain the following general expression for the mean time to human error:

$$
T_{\text {mhc }}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\left[e^{-\frac{1}{2} \gamma(t) d t}\right] d t
$$

### 10.6 Case Studies of Human Error in Aviation Maintenance

Over the years, many aircraft accidents due to human error in maintenance have occurred. Two of these accidents are briefly described below.# 10.6.1 British Airways BAC 1-11 Aircraft Accident 

This accident occurred on June 10, 1990 when a British Airways BAC 1-11 aircraft departed Birmingham International airport in the United Kingdom for Malaga, Spain with 81 passengers and 6 crew members on board. As the aircraft was climbing through 17,300 feet pressure altitude, a cockpit windscreen blown out and sucked out the pilot in command through the windscreen aperture [3].

Fortunately, the co-pilot immediately regained control of the aircraft and the cabin crew members held the pilot by the ankles until the landing of the aircraft. A subsequent investigation into the accident revealed that the cause of the accident was the fitting of a replacement windscreen by using incorrect bolts [3].

### 10.6.2 Continental Express Embraer Brasilia Accident

This accident occurred in September 1991 when a Continental Express Embraer Brasilia crashed, killing all on board, because the leading edge of the left horizontal stabilizer separated from the aircraft [2]. A subsequent investigation into the accident revealed that the night before the accident some maintenance work, involving the removal of screws from the upper left surface of the aircraft's "T-tail," was performed. When the shift change occurred, the work was only partially completed and it was not documented.

Unfortunately, maintenance technicians of the incoming shift, being unaware of the partial completion of the maintenance work, signed the aircraft back into service. In the final report on the accident, the National Transportation Safety Board highlighted deficient maintenance practices within the airline organization $[2,25]$.

### 10.7 Useful Guidelines to Reduce Human Error in Aircraft Maintenance

Over the years, various guidelines have been developed to reduce the occurrence of human error in aircraft maintenance. These guidelines cover the following ten areas [9]:

- Tools and equipment
- Procedures
- Design
- Human error risk management
- Towing aircraft
- Maintenance incident feedback
- Training
- Shift handover
- Communication
- SupervisionGuidelines associated with each of the above ten areas are presented below, separately. Two guidelines concerning tools and equipment are reviewing systems by which items such as stands and lighting systems are kept to remove unserviceable equipment from service and repairing it rapidly, and ensuring the storage of lock-out devices in such a way that it becomes immediately apparent when they are left in place inadvertently. Four guidelines concerning procedures are as follows:

- Review work practices on a regular basis to ensure that they do not differ significantly from formal procedures.
- Review checklist effectiveness in assisting the performance of aircraft maintenance people in routine circumstances such as preparing an aircraft for towing and activating hydraulics.
- Ensure that standard work practices are being followed throughout all maintenance operations.
- Review all documented maintenance procedures and practices on a regular basis with respect to their consistency, accessibility, and realism.

Two useful guidelines pertaining to design are actively seek relevant information on the occurrence of human errors during the maintenance phase to provide appropriate input in the design phase and ensure that all equipment manufacturers give adequate attention to maintenance-related human factors during the design phase. Three guidelines pertaining to human error risk management are as follows:

- Avoid carrying out simultaneously the same maintenance task on similar redundant items.
- Review formally the effectiveness of defences, such as engine runs, built into the system to detect maintenance errors.
- Review the need to disturb normally functioning systems for performing rather nonessential periodic maintenance inspections, because the disturbance may result in a maintenance error.

A useful guideline in the areas of towing aircraft or other equipment is, review the procedures and equipment used for towing to and from all maintenance facilities. Two guidelines in the area of maintenance incident feedback are as follows:

- Ensure that all appropriate personnel in management receive an effective feedback on human factors-related maintenance incidents periodically, with particular consideration to the underlying conditions that promote the occurrence of such incidents.
- Ensure that all personnel involved with training are given an effective feedback on recurring human factors-related maintenance incidents on a regular basis, so that appropriate corrective measures at these problems are targeted effectively.

### 11.2.2 Model II

This model is concerned with predicting the probability that a self-generated error will be corrected in time $t$. In Reference [1], the correctability function is defined as the probability that a task error will be corrected in time $t$ subjected to stress constraint associated with the task and its environment. Mathematically, the correctability function may be defined as follows:

$$
P_{\mathrm{c}}(t)=P(\text { correction of error in time } t / \text { stress })
$$where
$P \quad$ is the probability.
$P_{\mathrm{c}}(t) \quad$ is the probability that a human error will be corrected in time $t$.
The time derivative of not-correctability function, $\overline{P_{\mathrm{c}}}(t)$, may be defined as follows $[1,2]:$

$$
\overline{P^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{c}}(t)=-\frac{1}{N} \cdot N_{\mathrm{c}}^{\prime}(t)
$$

where the prime denotes differentiation with respect to time $t$, and
$N \quad$ is the total number of times task correction is accomplished after time $t$.
$N_{\bar{c}}(t) \quad$ is the total number of times the task is not accomplished after time $t$.
By dividing the both sides of Equation (11.10) by $N_{\bar{c}}(t)$, we get

$$
\frac{N \cdot \overline{P^{\prime}}{ }_{\mathrm{c}}(t)}{N_{\bar{c}}(t)}=-\frac{N_{\bar{c}}^{\prime}(t)}{N_{\bar{c}}(t)}
$$

The right-hand side of Equation (11.11) represents the instantaneous task correction rate $\gamma_{\mathrm{c}}(t)$. Hence, Equation (11.11) may be rewritten to the following form:

$$
\frac{\overline{P^{\prime}}{ }_{\mathrm{c}}(t)}{\overline{P_{\mathrm{c}}}^{\prime}(t)}+\gamma_{\mathrm{c}}(t)=0
$$

By solving Equation (11.12) for given initial conditions, we get

$$
\overline{P_{\mathrm{c}}}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-\int_{0}^{t} \gamma_{\mathrm{c}}(t) \mathrm{d} t}
$$

Since $P_{\mathrm{c}}(t)+\overline{P_{\mathrm{c}}}(t)=1$, we write

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_{\mathrm{c}}(t) & =1-\overline{P_{\mathrm{c}}}^{\prime}(t) \\
& =1-\mathrm{e}^{-\int_{0}^{t} \gamma_{\mathrm{c}}(t) \mathrm{d} t}
\end{aligned}
$$

It is to be noted that Equation (11.14) is a general expression that holds for both constant and non-constant task correction rates. More specifically, it holds whether the tasks correction rate is described by the exponential distribution or any other statistical distribution such as Rayleigh.

# 11.4.2 Model II 

This model is basically same as the previous model (i.e., Model I) but with one exception, i.e., the failed vehicle is repaired. More specifically, when the vehicle fails in the field, repair is attempted. If it cannot be repaired, then the vehicle is towed to the repair facility for repair. The redrawn diagram of Figure 11.3 is shown in Figure 11.4 with constant repair rates. Thus, Figure 11.4 is the state space diagram for this model. The assumptions associated with this model are the same as for Model I. The symbols used to denote vehicle repair rates are defined below.
$\mu_{0}$ is the constant repair rate of the vehicle from the repair workshop (i.e., state 3).
$\mu$ is the constant repair rate of the vehicle when failed in the field due to a hardware failure.
$\mu_{\mathrm{he}}$ is the constant repair rate of the vehicle when failed in the field due a human error.
Other symbols used in this model are the same as for Model I. By using the Markov method, we write down the following Equations for the Figure 11.4 diagram $[2,9]$ :

\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{1}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}+\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{y}}+\mu_{\mathrm{he}}\right) P_{1}(t)=\lambda_{\mathrm{he}} P_{0}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{2}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}+\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{x}}+\mu\right) P_{2}(t)=\lambda P_{0}(t) \\

This model represents an on-surface transit system (e.g., a vehicle) that can either fail safely or fail with accident due to human errors or hardware failures [2, 10]. The failed system is taken to the repair shop. After repair, it is put back into normal operation. The model state space diagram is shown in Figure 11.5 and the numerals in diagram circles and box denote system states. The model is subjected to the following assumptions:

- All failures and errors are statistically independent.
- Failure, human error, towing, and repair rates are constant.
- The repaired system is as good as new.

$i=2$ means that the vehicle has failed safely due to human errors,
$i=3$ means that the vehicle has failed with accident due to hardware failures,
$i=4$ means that the vehicle has failed with accident due to human errors,
$i=5$ means that the vehicle is in repair shop.

$\lambda_{\mathrm{b}} \quad$ is the constant vehicle safe-failure human error rate.

$\lambda_{\text {ha }} \quad$ is the constant human error rate of the vehicle that cause an accident.
$\lambda_{\mathrm{ti}} \quad$ is the constant vehicle towing rate from state $i$ to state 5 , for $i=1,2,3,4$.
$\mu \quad$ is the constant vehicle repair rate form state 5 to state 0 .

# 11.4 Models for Performing Human Error Analysis in Transportation Systems 

Over the years many mathematical models have been developed to perform various types of human error analysis in transportation systems [9-10]. This section presents three such models.

### 11.4.1 Model I

This model represents an on-surface transit system subjected to two types of failures: hardware failures and failures due to human errors [2, 9]. An example of such system is an operating vehicle that can fail either due to hardware failure or a failure


Figure 11.3. State space diagram for a vehicle failing due to a hardware failure or a human errorcaused by a human error. The failed vehicle is towed to the repair workshop. The state space diagram of the model is shown in Figure 11.3. The numerals in the diagram circle and boxes denote system states. The following assumptions are associated with the model:

- Failures and human errors occur independently.
- All failure rates are constant.
- The towing rates are constant.
- The vehicle can fail completely either due to hardware failures or due to human errors.

The following symbols are associated with the model:
$i$ is the $i$ th state of the on-surface transit system (i.e., vehicle); $i=0$ means that the vehicle operating normally, $i=1$ means that the vehicle has failed in the field due to a human error, $i=2$ means that the vehicle has failed in the field due to a hardware failure, $i=3$ means that the vehicle is in the repair workshop.
$P_{j}(t)$ is the probability that the on-surface transit system (i.e., vehicle) is in state $i$ at time $t$, for $i=0,1,2,3$.
$\lambda$ is the vehicle constant hardware failure rate.
$\lambda_{\text {he }}$ is the vehicle constant failure rate due to human errors.
$\lambda_{\mathrm{x}} \quad$ is the vehicle constant towing rate from system state 2 to state 3 .
$\lambda_{\mathrm{y}} \quad$ is the vehicle constant towing rate from system state 1 to state 3 .
With the aid of the Markov method, we write down the following equations for the Figure 11.3 diagram $[2,9,10]$ :

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{0}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}+\left(\lambda+\lambda_{\mathrm{he}}\right) P_{0}(t)=0 \\
\frac{\mathrm{~d} P_{1}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}+\lambda_{\mathrm{y}} P_{1}(t)=\lambda_{\mathrm{he}} P_{0}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{2}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}+\lambda_{\mathrm{y}} P_{2}(t)=\lambda P_{0}(t) \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} P_{3}(t)}{\mathrm{d} t}=\lambda_{\mathrm{x}} P_{2}(t)+\lambda_{\mathrm{y}} P_{1}(t)
\end{gathered}
$$

At time $t=0, P_{0}(0)=1$, and $P_{1}(0)=P_{3}(0)=P_{4}(0)=0$.
Solving Equations (11.45)-(11.48) by using Laplace transforms, we get

$$
P_{0}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-c t}
$$

where

$$
c=\lambda+\lambda_{\mathrm{he}}
$$$$
P_{1}(t)=c_{1}\left(\mathrm{e}^{-c t}-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{v} t}\right)
$$

where

$$
\begin{gathered}
c_{1}=\lambda_{\mathrm{he}} /\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{y}}-c\right) \\
P_{2}(t)=c_{2}\left(\mathrm{e}^{-c t}-\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{x}} t}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

where

$$
\begin{gathered}
c_{2}=\lambda /\left(\lambda_{\mathrm{x}}-c\right) \\
P_{3}(t)=1+c_{1} \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{v} t}+c_{2} \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_{v} t}+c_{3} \mathrm{e}^{-c t}
\end{gathered}
$$

where

$$
c_{3}=-\left(c_{1} \lambda_{y}+c_{2} \lambda_{x}\right) / c
$$

The vehicle or transit system reliability is given by

$$
R_{v}(t)=P_{0}(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-c t}
$$

where
$R_{v}(t)$ is the vehicle or transit system reliability at time $t$.
The vehicle mean time to failure is given by [7]

$$
\begin{aligned}
M T T F_{\mathrm{v}} & =\int_{0}^{\infty} R_{\mathrm{v}}(t) \mathrm{d} t \\
& =\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{e}^{-c t} \mathrm{~d} t \\
& =\frac{1}{c}=\frac{1}{\lambda+\lambda_{\mathrm{he}}}
\end{aligned}
$$

where
$M T T F_{v}$ is the vehicle mean time to failure.

# 8.1.2.3 Maximization of Expected Total Number of Consecutive Jobs Completed During the Field Operation 

Let the components in field operation consecutively perform 'jobs' of the same nature. # 8.3.3 Optimal Burn-in Based on Conservative Measures 

Failures of items may often result in the catastrophic or disastrous events. For example, failures in jet engines of aircrafts or those in gas safety valves may cause fatal consequences. Similarly, failures during important missions can cause huge economic loss. In these cases, rather than the 'average quality' of the heterogeneous population, which (as in the previous sections) we understand as $\lambda_{m}(t)$, it is reasonable to define the 'marginal' quality in the population that refers in some sense to the "worst scenario". That is, if this marginal quality is still acceptable, then the quality of our population as a whole should also be considered as satisfactory. This reasoning can create an alternative approach to the one discussed inFig. $8.23 \Phi(b)$

the previous subsections. The marginal quality can be used as a conservative measure (or bound) for the population quality. In this subsection, we consider the optimal burn-in procedures that optimize the conservative measures for continuous mixture models.

After burn-in during time $b$, the components in the population will have the failure rate $\lambda(t+b, z)$ in accordance with the conditional frailty distribution $\pi(z \mid b)$ defined in Sect. 8.3.2. Thus, we can define the following ' $x$ th worst' realization of the 'residual' failure rate in the population:

$$
\lambda_{\alpha}(t \mid b)=\lambda(b+t, z(\alpha \mid b)), t \geq 0
$$

where $z(\alpha \mid b) \equiv \inf \left\{z: \prod(z \mid b) \geq \alpha\right\}$ and $\alpha$ is usually close to 1 (e.g., 0.9 or 0.95 ) and, as previously, $\Pi(z \mid b)$ is the conditional distribution function, which corresponds to the conditional pdf $\pi(z \mid b)$. Accordingly, $\lambda_{\alpha}(t \mid b)$ is the failure rate of an item that has survived burn-in during time $b$, which corresponds to the $\alpha$ th percentile $z(\alpha \mid b)$ of the conditional distribution of frailty $\prod(z \mid b)$. When $\alpha$ is close to 1 , this can be interpreted as the $\alpha$ th worst scenario. Based on the above setting, we can define the $\alpha$ th worst MRL of the population after the burn-in time $b$ :

$$
M_{\alpha}(b) \equiv \int_{0}^{\infty} \exp \left\{-\int_{0}^{t} \lambda_{\alpha}(u \mid b) \mathrm{d} u\right\} \mathrm{d} t
$$

Therefore, the following criterion can be applied:
Criterion 3 Determine the optimal burn-in time $b^{*}$ as the minimal burn-in time $b$, such that $M_{\alpha}(b) \geq m_{r}$, where $m_{r}$ is the MRL that corresponds to the $\alpha$ th worst scenario.

In the framework of our burn-in model, consider now the corresponding gains and penalties defined for four mutually exclusive events. Denote:

- $g_{1}$ : gain due to the survival of a strong component
- $c_{1}$ : penalty incurred by the elimination of a strong component
- $g_{2}$ : gain due to the elimination of a weak component
- $c_{2}$ : penalty incurred by the survival of a weak component.

In accordance with this notation and relationship (9.4), the expected gain resulting from the burn-in procedure performed by a shock is given by the following function of severity $s$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
\varphi(s) & =g_{1} \pi \bar{G}(s)+g_{2}(1-\pi) G(\rho(s))-c_{1} \pi G(s)-c_{2}(1-\pi) \bar{G}(\rho(s)) \\
& =-\left(\pi g_{1}+\pi c_{1}\right) G(s)+\left((1-\pi) g_{2}+(1-\pi) c_{2}\right) G(\rho(s))+g_{1} \pi-c_{2}(1-\pi)
\end{aligned}
$$

It is clear that maximization of $\varphi(s)$ is equivalent to minimization of

$$
\pi\left(g_{1}+c_{1}\right) G(s)+(1-\pi)\left(g_{2}+c_{2}\right)(1-G(\rho(s)))
$$

or to minimization of

$$
\psi(s) \equiv w_{1} G(s)+w_{2}(1-G(\rho(s)))
$$

where the weights $w_{1}$ and $w_{2}$ are

$$
w_{1}=\frac{\pi\left(g_{1}+c_{1}\right)}{\pi\left(g_{1}+c_{1}\right)+(1-\pi)\left(g_{2}+c_{2}\right)}, w_{2}=1-w_{1}
$$

Note that the probability of failure of a strong component $G(s)$ can be interpreted as the risk that the strong component will be eliminated by a shock. On the other hand, $(1-G(\rho(s))$ can be regarded as the risk that a weak component will survive a shock. Expressions (9.8) and (9.9) imply that maximization of expected gain is equivalent to minimization of the weighted risk. Observe that when $s=0, \psi(0)=$ $w_{2}$ and when $s \rightarrow \infty, \psi(\infty)=w_{1}$.The optimal severity $s^{*}$ should be obtained numerically, however, we can define an upper bound for $s^{*}$ under some additional conditions.

# 9.2.4 The Cost of Burn-in and Optimal Problem 

In field operation, items are frequently required to survive a pre-specified time period, which is called the mission time, $\tau$. In this subsection, optimal severity of a shock, which minimizes the average cost incurred during the burn-in and the operation phase will be considered.As previously, a new component randomly selected from the heterogeneous population is burned-in by means of a shock. If the first one did not survive then we take another one from infinite heterogeneous population and burn-in again. This procedure is repeated until we obtain the first component which survives burn-in. Then this component is put into the field operation. Assume, first, for simplicity, that the cost of conducting a single shock $c_{s}=0$. Denote by $c_{1}$ the expected cost of the burn-in until obtaining the first item that has survived shocks. It is clear that

$$
\begin{aligned}
c_{1} & =0 \times(1-P)+c_{s r} P(1-P)+2 c_{s r} P^{2}(1-P)+3 c_{s r} P^{3}(1-P)+\cdots \\
& =c_{s r} P(1-P)\left(1+2 P+3 P^{2}+\cdots\right)=\frac{c_{s r} P}{1-P}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_{s r}$ is the shop replacement cost. Similarly, when $c_{s} \neq 0$

$$
c_{1}=\frac{c_{s r} P+c_{s}}{1-P}
$$

Obviously, this function increases when $P$ increases in $[0,1)$. Note that $P$ is now a function of the stress level $s$, that is, $P(s)$ [see definition (9.31), where $p(z)$ should be substituted by $p(z, s)$ ] and thus, in the following, $c_{1}$ in (9.34) and (9.35) should be also understood as a function of $s, c_{1}(s)$.

The cost $c_{m}$ is incurred by the event $\left\{T_{s} \leq \tau\right\}$ (Failure of the Mission);
The gain $g_{m}$ results from the event $\left\{T_{s}>\tau\right\}$ (Success of the Mission).

$$

Consider now the second criterion. Let $\tau$ be the usage (mission) time for our components. Based on the foregoing results, we can also consider now certain cost structures for determining the optimal severity level. As previously, an item is chosen at random from our initial population and during the ESS it is exposed to a shock of magnitude $s$. If it survives, it is put into field operation, otherwise the failed item is discarded and a new one is chosen from the population, etc. This procedure is repeated until the first survived item is obtained. Let $c_{s r}$ be the shop replacement cost (actually, it is the cost of a new item) and $c_{s}$ be the cost for conducting the ESS. Let $c_{1}(s)$, as a function of $s$, be the expected cost for eventually obtaining a component which has survived the ESS. Then

$$
c_{1}(s)=\frac{c_{s}+c_{s r}\left[1-\left\{\pi+(1-\alpha(s)) P\left(R>W_{s}\right)(1-\pi)\right\}\right]}{\pi+(1-\alpha(s)) P\left(R>W_{s}\right)(1-\pi)}
$$

where $1 /\left\{\pi+(1-\alpha(s)) P\left(R>W_{s}\right)(1-\pi)\right\}$ is the total number of trials until the first 'success'.

In field operation, assume that if the mission (of length $\tau$ ) is successful, then a gain $K$ is given; otherwise a penalty $C$ is imposed, where $K>C>0$. Then the expected gain during field operation (until failure) is given by

$$
c_{2}(s)=-K \bar{F}_{E}(\tau ; s)+C F_{E}(\tau ; s)=-(K+C) \bar{F}_{E}(\tau ; s)+C
$$

and the total expected cost $c(s)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
c(s) & =c_{1}(s)+c_{2}(s) \\
& =\frac{c_{s}+c_{s r}\left[1-\left\{\pi+(1-\alpha(s)) P\left(R>W_{s}\right)(1-\pi)\right\}\right]}{\pi+(1-\alpha(s)) P\left(R>W_{s}\right)(1-\pi)}-(K+C) \bar{F}_{E}(\tau ; s)+C
\end{aligned}
$$

The objective is to find the optimal severity level $s^{*}$ that satisfies

$$
s^{*}=\arg \min _{s \in[0, \infty]} c(s)
$$Similar to Theorem 10.5, if $\rho(\infty) \equiv \lim _{s \rightarrow \infty} \rho(s)>(1-\pi)$ then the optimal severity level which minimizes $c_{2}(s)$ (maximizes $\bar{F}_{E}(\tau ; s)$, as follows from (10.15)) does not exist in the interval $\left(s_{0}, \infty\right)$. Furthermore, $c_{1}(s)$ is strictly increasing to infinity. Therefore, we can conclude that the optimal severity level $s^{*}$ should exist in the interval $\left[0, s_{0}\right]$.

Assume now that during field operation, the gain is proportional to the mean time to failure. Therefore, the total average cost function in this case is

$$
c(s)=\frac{c_{s}+c_{s r}\left[1-\left\{\pi+(1-\alpha(s)) P\left(R>W_{s}\right)(1-\pi)\right\}\right]}{\pi+(1-\alpha(s)) P\left(R>W_{s}\right)(1-\pi)}-K \int_{0}^{\infty} \bar{F}_{E}(t ; s) \mathrm{d} t
$$

By the similar arguments, the optimal severity level $s^{*}$ should exist in the interval $\left[0, s_{0}\right]$.

# (2) Optimum $N^{*}$ 

Suppose that a unit is replaced at shock $N(N=1,2, \cdots)$ or at failure, whichever occurs first. Then, the expected cost rate is, from (3.8),

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_{2}(N) & \equiv \lim _{\substack{T \rightarrow \infty \\
Z \rightarrow K}} C(T, N, Z) \\
& =\frac{c_{K}-\left(c_{K}-c_{N}\right) G^{(N)}(K)}{(1 / \lambda) \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} G^{(j)}(K)} \quad(N=1,2, \cdots)
\end{aligned}
$$

In particular, when $N=1$, i.e., the unit is always replaced at the first shock, the expected cost rate is

$$
C_{2}(1)=\lambda\left[c_{K}-\left(c_{K}-c_{N}\right) G(K)\right]
$$Forming the inequality $C_{2}(N+1)-C_{2}(N) \geq 0$ to seek an optimum number $N^{*}$ that minimizes $C_{2}(N)$ for $c_{K}>c_{N}$,

$$
Q_{2}(N+1) \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} G^{(j)}(K)-\left[1-G^{(N)}(K)\right] \geq \frac{c_{N}}{c_{K}-c_{N}} \quad(N=1,2, \cdots)
$$

where

$$
Q_{2}(N) \equiv \frac{G^{(N-1)}(K)-G^{(N)}(K)}{G^{(N-1)}(K)} \quad(N=1,2, \cdots)
$$

If $Q_{2}(N)$ is strictly increasing in $N$, i.e., $G^{(j+1)}(x) / G^{(j)}(x)$ is strictly decreasing in $j$, then the left-hand side of (3.22) is also strictly increasing in $N$ to $Q_{2}(\infty)\left[1+M_{G}(K)\right]-1$, where $Q_{2}(\infty) \equiv \lim _{N \rightarrow \infty} Q_{2}(N) \leq 1$. Thus, if $Q_{2}(\infty)\left[1+M_{G}(K)\right]>c_{K} /\left(c_{K}-c_{N}\right)$, then there exists a finite and unique minimum number $N^{*}\left(1 \leq N^{*}<\infty\right)$ that satisfies (3.22), and the expected cost rate is

$$
\lambda\left(c_{K}-c_{N}\right) Q_{2}\left(N^{*}\right)<C_{2}\left(N^{*}\right) \leq \lambda\left(c_{K}-c_{N}\right) Q_{2}\left(N^{*}+1\right)
$$

Conversely, if $Q_{2}(\infty)\left[1+M_{G}(K)\right] \leq c_{K} /\left(c_{K}-c_{N}\right)$, then $N^{*}=\infty$. Note that $Q_{2}(N)$ corresponds to the discrete failure rate $r_{N}$ given in (2.15), and $Q_{2}(N+1)$ represents the probability that the unit surviving at the $N$ th shock will fail at the $(N+1)$ th shock. In general, $Q_{2}(N)$ would increase to 1 . In this case, if $M_{G}(K)>c_{N} /\left(c_{K}-c_{N}\right)$, i.e., the expected number of shocks before failure is greater than $c_{N} /\left(c_{K}-c_{N}\right)$, then a finite $N^{*}$ exists uniquely.

# 3.3 Modified Replacement Models 

This section considers some extended models of Section 3.1 in more general replacement forms and discusses optimum policies. Furthermore, we propose the combined preventive replacement models of planned time, shock number and damage level. These models would be more realistic than the basic ones, and moreover, offer interesting topics to reliability theoreticians.# (1) Modified Cost 

The replacement costs may depend on the damage level at its replacement time. It is assumed that $c_{0}(x)(0 \leq x \leq K)$ is an additional replacement cost that is variable for the total damage $x$ with $c(0)=0$, that is, $\operatorname{cost} c_{k}+c_{0}(x)$ $(k=T, N, Z)$ is incurred for the replacement of the unit with damage $x$ at time $T$, shock $N$, and damage $Z$, respectively, and $\operatorname{cost} c_{K}+c_{0}(K)$ is incurred for the replacement at failure.

The expected cost when the unit is replaced at time $T$ is

F_{N}(T) \int_{0}^{Z}\left[c_{N}+c_{0}(x)\right] \mathrm{d} G^{(N)}(x)

$$

# 4.2.2 Model 2: Shock Damage 

Whenever unit 1 fails, it acts as some shock to unit 2 and causes an amount of damage with distribution $G(x)$ to unit 2 . The total damage is additive and unit 2 fails whenever it has exceeded a failure level $K$. The system is replaced at the failure of unit 2 or at the $N$ th failure of unit 1 , whichever occurs first.

The probability that the system is replaced at the $N$ th failure of unit 1 is $G^{(N)}(K)$, where $G^{(j)}(x)(j=1,2, \cdots)$ is the $j$-fold Stieltjes convolution of $G(x)$ with itself and $G^{(0)}(x) \equiv 1$ for $x \geq 0$. Thus, the mean time to replacement is, from (3.5),

$$
\sum_{j=0}^{N-1} G^{(j)}(K) \int_{0}^{\infty} p_{j}(t) \mathrm{d} t

### 2.2.1 Random Variables and Distribution Functions

## Random Variable

In conducting experiments, we are often more interested in some functions of the outcome than the outcome itself. Suppose that an electronic device consists of three key components, and if any one of the three components breaks, the device will be disposed. If we want to know the average life of this device, we should know the life of the component, which is the minimum of the three, and we will not be concerned about the lives of the other two. In other words, we will be interested in knowing that the minimum is 9.2 months, and not be concerned if the lives of the other two are $(10.3,12.6)$ or $(10.5,18.3)$, etc.

As shown in the above example, the values of interest are defined as random variables. Formally a random variable is defined as real valued functions defined on the sample space. This definition indicates that since a rand

vents, denoted by $\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} E_{i}$ is defined as the event consisting of all the outcomes of the events $E_{1}, E_{2}, \ldots, E_{n}$ while their intersection, denoted by $\bigcap_{i=1}^{n} E_{i}$ is the event consisting of those outcomes common in all the events $E_{1}, E_{2}, \ldots, E_{n}$. The complement of $E$, often denoted by $E^{\mathrm{c}}$ or $\overline{\mathrm{E}}$, is defined as the event consisting of all the outcomes in the sample space, which do not belong to $E$. In the example of tossing a coin, the sample space $S=$ $\{\mathrm{H}, \mathrm{T}\}$. If event $E$ were one head, then $E^{\mathrm{c}}$ would be one tail. Based on the notion of set and experiment, we can now define the concept of probability.

There are a couple of major perspectives on the concept of probability. The classical perspective takes the ratio of the number of successes to the total number of trials:

$$
P(\text { success })=\frac{\text { number of successes }}{\text { total number of trials }}
$$

This perspective is conceptually easy to understand. However, it has some ambiguities that limit its wider application: it is not often possible to repeat the experiment, and even if it could be repeated, it's not clear how many times we need to repeat the experiment in order to obtain the exact probability.

The other important perspective is the axiomatic probability. It is based on the following three axioms.
(i) $0 \leq P(E) \leq 1$
(ii) $P(S)=1$
(iii) If events $E_{1}, E_{2}, \ldots, E_{n}$ are mutually exclusive, $P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} E_{i}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} P\left(E_{i}\right)$

Since it is simple to use and mathematically clear, it is widely applied in analysis. We will take this perspective for our discussion on probabilities. In this context, the probability of an event can be defined as a quantitative measure over a $0-1$ scale, representing the frequency of the occurrence of the event relative to the sample space. Further, the probability of an event $E$ is the sum of the probabilities of the elements in $E$. In terms of the probabilities, uncertaintytakes place when the sample space has more than one element with nonzero probability of occurrence, which prevents us from predicting the outcome of an experiment.

# 2.1.2 Rules of Probability

In order to calculate the probabilities of a specific or combination of events, we need to understand some basic rules or properties of probabilities. We can derive the following properties of probability based on the probability axioms in (2.2).

Since $E$ and $E^{\mathrm{c}}$ are mutually exclusive, and $E \cup E^{\mathrm{c}}=S$ by definition,

$$
P\left(E \cup E^{\mathrm{c}}\right)=P(S)=P(E)+P\left(E^{\mathrm{c}}\right)=1
$$

For any two given events $A$ and $B$, the probability of the union of $A$ and $B$, that is the probability of any one of the events $A$ and $B$ taking place is calculated by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B) \\
& \quad=P(A)+P(B)-P(A B)
\end{aligned}
$$

since all points in $A \cap B$ are counted twice in $P(A)+P(B)$.
In the case where we calculate the probability of the union of three events $A, B$, and $C$, we can see the following

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P(A \cup B \cup C)=P[(A \cup B) \cup C]=P(A \cup B)+P(C)-P[(A \cup B) C] \\
& \quad=P(A)+P(B)-P(A B)+P(C)-P(A C \cup B C) \\
& \quad=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)-P(A B)-P(B C)-P(A C)+P(A B C)
\end{aligned}
$$

The above calculation process can be extended in the case of union of multiple events $E_{1}, E_{2}$, $\ldots, E_{n}$. By induction, we can obtain,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P\left[\bigcup_{i=1}^{n} E_{i}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n} P\left(E_{i}\right)-\sum_{i<j}^{n} P\left(E_{i} E_{j}\right)+\sum_{i<j<k}^{n} P\left(E_{i} E_{j} E_{k}\right) \\
& \quad-\sum_{i<j<k<l}^{n} P\left(E_{i} E_{j} E_{k} E_{l}\right)+\ldots+(-1)^{n+1} P\left(E_{1} E_{2} \ldots E_{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

# Weibull Distribution

We say that a random variable X has a Weibull distribution with a scale parameter $\mu$, and a shape parameter $\beta$, if its density function is given by


$$

f(x)=\left\{\frac{\beta}{\mu} \left\|\frac{x}{\mu}\right\|^{\beta-1} \exp \left[-\left(\frac{x}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right]\right\} \quad x \geq 0

$$

If the Weibull random variable X shifts left or right from 0 , we can redefine the density function of the Weibull distribution with one more parameter $v$, the location parameter $(-\infty<v<\infty)$ as follows.


$$

f(x)=\left\{\frac{\beta}{\mu} \left\|\frac{x-v}{\mu}\right\|^{\beta-1} \exp \left[-\left(\frac{x-v}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right]\right\} \quad x \geq v

$$

The location parameter does not affect the variance. This modification is often referred to as the Three Parameter (3-P) Weibull Distribution or Modified Weibull Distribution.

The cdf of the 3-P Weibull distribution is derived as


$$

F(x)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { if } x<v \\ 1-\exp \left[-\left(\frac{x-v}{\mu}\right)^{\beta}\right] & \text { if } x \geq v\end{cases}

$$

Fig. 2.3(d) shows some density functions of the Weibull distribution when $v=0$. As shown by the Figure, we can generate many different shapes by manipulating the values of the two parameters $\mu$ and $\beta$. Thus, the Weibull distribution provides us with convenience to fit experimental data. It can be shown easily when $\mu=\frac{1}{\lambda}, \beta=1$, and $v=0$, the density function would be $f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$. This is the same as the density function of the exponential distribution. Therefore, we can say that the exponential distribution is a special case of the Weibull distribution. The reader should note that different authors use various notations for the parameters in the Weibull distribution.

# Exponential Distribution

We say that a random variable $X$ has an exponential distribution with parameter $\lambda$ if its density function is given by


$$

f(x)= \begin{cases}\lambda \exp (-\lambda x) & \text { if } x \geq 0 \\ 0 & \text { if } x<0\end{cases}

$$

The exponential distribution is often denoted by $\exp (\lambda)$. The parameter implies the rate of the occurrence in the event that the random variable $X$ represents. Fig. 2.3(b) shows the density functions of the exponential distribution when $\lambda=1$ and $\lambda=2$. The exponential distribution is widely applied in the analysis of the life of systems.


Figure 2.3 Pdfs of Some Continuous Probability DistributionsExample 2.9 Suppose that a random variable $X$ represents the life of a component, and it is exponentially distributed with parameter $\lambda$. What is the probability that this component will survive at least $s$ hours more, given that it has already survived $t$ hours so far?

Solution: Since $t+s>t$, we have,


$$

P(X>t+s \mid X>t)=\frac{P(X>t+s)}{P(X>t)}

$$

For any $t(t \geq 0)$, we have,


$$

P(X>t)=1-P(X \leq t)=1-\int\_{0}^{t} \lambda e^{-\lambda x} d x=1-\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)=e^{-\lambda t}

$$

Thus, it follows that,


$$

P(X>t+s \mid X>t)=\frac{e^{-\lambda(t+s)}}{e^{-\lambda t}}=e^{-\lambda s}=P(X>s)

$$

This equation shows that the probability that the component survives at least $s$ additional hours, given that it has already survived $t$ hours, is the same as the probability that it survives at least s hours. The distribution of the remaining life of the component is independent of the time used, so it is 'memoryless'. Therefore, a random variable with this property is said to have a memoryless property. It was proven that the exponential distribution is the only distribution with this property (Ross 1993).

# 2.3.3 Extreme Value Distribution

In dealing with the reliability of a system, we may face many situations where the extreme value(minimum or maximum) of a set of random variables will be our primary interest. In this section, we will explore the distribution and the density of the minimum and maximum of random variables.

Suppose that $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent random variables with distribution functions $F_{1}, F_{2}, \ldots, F_{n}$, respectively, and, $Y$ is the random variable that is the maximum of those $n$ variables. Then, let's calculate the distribution function $F_{y}(y)$ of $Y$.


$$

F*{Y}(y)=P(Y \leq y)=P\left[\left(X*{1} \leq y\right) \cap\left(X*{2} \leq y\right) \cap \ldots \cap\left(X*{n} \leq y\right)\right]

$$

Since $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent, we have,


$$

F*{Y}(y)=\prod*{i=1}^{n} P\left(X*{i} \leq y\right)=\prod*{i=1}^{n} F\_{i}(y)

$$

If all the $n$ random variables are identically distributed with a distribution function $F(x)$, we have,


$$

F\_{Y}(y)=F^{n}(y)

$$

It follows that the density function of $Y$ can be derived by


$$

f*{Y}(y)=\frac{d F*{Y}(y)}{d y}=n F^{n-1}(y) f(y)

$$

where $f(y)=\frac{d F(y)}{d y}$
The distribution of the minimum of random variables can be derived by a similar approach. Let $Z$ be the random variable that is the minimum of $n$ independent random variables $X_{1}, X_{2}$, $X_{3}, \ldots, X_{n}$.


$$

\begin{aligned}
& F*{Z}(z)=P(Z \leq z)=1-P(Z>z) \\
& \quad=1-P\left[\left(X*{1}>z\right) \cap\left(X*{2}>z\right) \cap \ldots \cap\left(X*{n}>z\right)\right]
\end{aligned}

$$

Since $X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, \ldots, X_{n}$ are independent,


$$

\begin{aligned}
& F*{Z}(z)=1-\prod*{i=1}^{n} P\left(X*{i}>z\right)=1-\prod*{i=1}^{n}\left[1-P\left(X_{i} \leq z\right)\right] \\
& \quad=1-\prod*{i=1}^{n}\left[1-F*{i}(z)\right]
\end{aligned}

$$

Thus, if these $n$ variables are identically distributed with the distribution function $F(x)$, we have


$$

F\_{Z}(z)=1-[1-F(z)]^{n}

$$

It follows that the density function of $Z$ can be derived by


$$

f*{Z}(z)=\frac{d F*{Z}(z)}{d z}=n[1-F(z)]^{n-1} f(z)

$$

where $f(z)=\frac{d F(z)}{d z}$# 2.3.4 Laws of Large Numbers

Suppose that $\left\{X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, \ldots,\right\}$ is the sequence of outcomes in an experiment where $X_{i}$ is the outcome of the $i$-th trial and each trial is conducted under identical conditions. Since each event $\left\{X_{i} \mid i=1,2, \ldots\right\}$ in this experiment is independent to each other, $\left\{X_{1}, X_{2}, X_{3}, \ldots,\right\}$ is a sequence of independent trials. One of the main objectives in repeating trials in an experiment in scientific research is to obtain insights into the eternal truth of the phenomena with a prospect that the result will proceed closer to the truth as the number of trials increases. In this section, we will study the behavior of probability distributions for random variables, which are the outcomes of an experiment where the number of trials goes to infinity. Before moving into the limiting behavior of distributions, we will first explore some of the conditions of the probability distributions, which will provide us with useful insights into the boundaries on probabilities when information on only the mean or both the mean and the variance is available.

## Markov Inequality

Let $X$ be a nonnegative random variable. Then, for any positive value $a$,


$$

P(X \geq a) \leq \frac{E[X]}{a}

$$

This inequality provides a good upper bound for the probability $P(X \geq a)$ when the value of $a$ is greater than $E[X]$.

## Chebyshev Inequality

Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$. Then, for any positive value $k$,


$$

P[|X-\mu| \geq k] \leq \frac{\sigma^{2}}{k^{2}}

$$

This inequality holds when the mean and variance are finite.

## Strong Law of Large Numbers

Let $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$. Then, with a probability of 1 ,


$$

\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} X\_{i}}{n}=\mu

$$

In other words, this law states that the average of a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables will converge to the mean of the distribution with a probability of 1 .

## Central Limit Theorem

Let $X_{1}, X_{2}, \ldots$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with finite mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$. Then, as $n$ goes to infinity,


$$

P\left[Z=\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} \leq a\right] \rightarrow \int*{-\infty}^{a} \frac{e^{-x^{2} / 2}}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} d x
$$where $\bar{X}$ the mean of the $n$ samples $X*{1}, X*{2}, \ldots, X*{n}$.
In other words, if the number of samples n is sufficiently large, the distribution of the sample mean tends toward a Normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and variance $\frac{\mu}{n}$ regardless of the original distribution of $\left\{X_{i}\right\}$. This theorem explains why the distribution of many random variables found in real life looks similar to the normal distribution. The Central Limit Theorem and the Strong Law of Large Numbers together provide the theoretical basis of using sample mean in the estimation for statistical analysis.

# Minimum Cut Set

A cut set is a set (or collection) of component failures that will produce system failure, and a minimum cut set is a cut set that has no subsets that are cut sets. This means that a minimum cut set is the limiting case of a cut set, i.e. it is a set of component failures that will produce system failure, with the further property that any single repair is sufficient to bring the system back to the functioning condition again. A list of all the minimum cut sets of a system tells the designer or user all there is to know about the reliability structure of the system, and if the data are available, the probability of failure of the system can be calculated. The probability of occurrence of each cut set is the product of the failure probabilities of each component in the set, and the failure probability of the system is the sum of the probabilities of occurrence of each cut set.

# 5.4 Fatigue Models

Fatigue modeling of components is essential to designing reliable components. There are three different approaches to fatigue modeling. These include the S-N Diagram, the MansonCoffin Equation and Linear Elastic Fracture Mechanics. We will review the basic elements of each of these in turn.

### 5.4.1 S-N Diagrams for Materials

Let's begin our discussion of fatigue models with the simplest approach. The S-N diagram is easiest to understand and manipulate and is widely used for design purposes. The S-N diagram is created by plotting the log of cycles to failure versus the log of the stress amplitude created by the fluctuating load. Let's initially consider a rotating bending test on small materials characterization samples of low alloy steel with polished surfaces. If we test several conditions recording the cycles to failure, we can construct a plot of mean cycles to failure versus applied stress amplitude. We will observe the characteristics shown in Figure 5.9.

Figure 5.9 S-N Curve that would be typical of a low alloy steel.

On the S-N diagram, we will define the stress amplitude for $N_{f}$ cycles to failure. We will also adopt $S$ for stress. We then define the fatigue strength, $S_{f}$ as the alternating stress causing failure at $N_{f}$ cycles and $S_{e}$ as the notation for the endurance limit. These are common notations used in design of mechanical components when using the S-N diagram.

The S-N curve can be characterized by three distinct regions. From 1 cycle to approximately $10^{3}$ cycles is the region of low cycle fatigue in which the applied stress amplitude results in relatively short life. A break point or change in slope will occur at about $10^{3}$ cycles. From this point, until approximately $10^{6}$ cycles, we have a region of high cycle fatigue in which the applied stress amplitude produces longer, but limited life. Beyond $10^{6}$ cycles, we can see that the applied stress amplitude approaches a constant value and does not limit the life of the material. This point, at which we transition to infinite life, is known as the endurance limit, $S_{e}$.

The S-N curve approach to modeling fatigue behavior in design of structural components is usually applied to the high cycle regime. We should also note that not all materials will have an endurance limit. Most non-ferrous materials will not have a distinct endurance limit. However, we can see that it may be desirable to design a steel structural component with infinite life, provided we can tolerate the extra weight and cost and appropriately measure the endurance limit.

The straight line behavior from $10^{3}$ to $10^{6}$ cycles on the S-N Diagram is often represented by the following simple power law relationship:


$$

S*{f}=C N*{f}^{b}

$$

where, C and b are materials properties and $N_{f}$ is the number of cycles to failure. The two constants can be extracted from our S-N Diagram.

As we can imagine, the fatigue life at $10^{0}$ cycles will closely correlate to the ultimate strength of the material. In fact, as previously discussed, $\frac{1}{2}$ cycle is a single stress reversal. This is approximately the condition of a tensile test. So, we can expect that the ultimate strength, $\sigma_{u}$, to approximate the fatigue strength at a single stress reversal.The break point at $10^{3}$ cycles is often taken as a fraction of the ultimate strength for estimating the high cycle $\mathrm{S}-\mathrm{N}$ curve for a small rotating bending test specimen. For steels, the average value is approximately 0.8 of the ultimate strength, $\sigma_{u}$. The lower limit may be estimated at $0.65 \sigma_{u}$. Also for steels, the endurance limit is approximately $0.5 \sigma_{u}$. These estimating values, however, should not be used to replace test data for the purposes of component design.

They will occur in components when a system encounters externally induced vibration, such as in the suspension of an automobile or the fluctuations of a printed wiring board assembly during take-off and landing of an aircraft. Rotating components are also subject to cyclic loads, including bearings, shafts and gears. Cyclic loads also occur as a result of temperature changes during operation of systems. The mean stress is $\sigma_{\text {mean }}$. When $\sigma_{\text {mean }}=0$, we have fully reversed loading and the stresses will include compressive stresses. Its important to note that crack growth will halt when the driving normal stress becomes compressive and the crack surfaces close together.

The stress ratio, $R$, is defined as:

Fatigue characterization is often conducted under these conditions on test samples. However, loading on actual components in the field may be significantly different. A complex load spectrum may look more like Figure 5.6.

In general, for reliability assessment, we test materials under simple loading spectra. Component loading conditions are then carefully evaluated and the stresses in the component are modelled. We then compare the stress conditions in the component to materials test data, to evaluate the life of the component. Components may also be tested to ensure their integrity. Fracture characteristics are also analyzed following tests.

In evaluating a complex loading spectra, we must define an additional term. A reversal occurs each time the direction of the load changes. For a simple cycle we define two reversals per cycle. Hence, the number of reversals to failure is twice the number of cycles to failure. This is a simple concept but important in trying to deal with complex spectra and modeling fatigue in real components.

Figure 5.6 A complex loading spectrum for a component.# 5.3 Fatigue Tests

There are several methods of executing fatigue tests for characterizing materials. ASTM standards define specimens and conditions for executing theses tests. Two common methods for which data are reported, include the rotating bending test and the axial fatigue test.

### 5.3.1 Test Methods

The rotating bending test is rather simple and involves applying a single direction load to a rotating specimen. This results in fully reversed bending loads, as the specimen rotates. The number of cycles to fracture the specimen is recorded. A simple test jig is shown schematically in Figure 5.7.

Axial tests usually involve more complex equipment. Hydraulic test equipment is used to apply an axial load to a specimen. This type of testing can be much more versatile. Mean stresses can be applied. In addition, twisting loads can be combined to evaluate multi-axial stresses. Load and deflection can be controlled. Failure can be defined as being a fraction of load reduction under a constant deflection.

Specimen configuration is an important issue in fatigue testing. Materials characterization is usually performed on specimens with a polished surface. Recall that fatigue crack initiation is associated with the surface condition. A polished surface is ideal and will not represent many components. The manufacturing processes used to fabricate components will significantly effect the surface condition. This results a reduction in fatigue life of the component in comparison to materials characterization test data.

Tests may also be conducted on components. Testing conducted at the component level, usually requires specialized equipment. Components may be significantly larger and complex in shape. Test equipment must be capable of applying a representative load. Component level testing can therefore be much more expensive then materials characterization tests performed on smaller standardized specimens.

### 5.3.2 Fatigue Test Data Analysis

Fatigue data will generally show significant variations, for a given test condition. The most uniform specimens may exhibit large variations in fatigue life. This indicates the importance of materials property variations and their influence on fatigue life. Testing of components

Figure 5.7 Diagram of a simple rotating bending test jig.will exhibit even larger variations in the fatigue life. This reflects the added influence of manufacturing process variation on the component fatigue life.

Variations in fatigue life are often described by the Weibull distribution. The number of cycles to failure are recorded for the samples. The data are then plotted on Weibull probability plots. Plotting techniques for test data are discussed in detail in Chapter 12. Fatigue data are sometimes represented by the lognormal distribution as well. The best fit distribution must be determined from a Goodness of Fit Test. Variation in fatigue data are shown in Figure 5.8 for a given load condition.

The Weibull distribution is appealing for fatigue, as it is an appropriate distribution to represent the probability of the weakest link failing. The weakest link in a materials test specimen, may be the point where we encounter the largest materials defect or where the grains of the polycrystalline metal are aligned favourably for slip processes to initiate a crack. Hence, we see that the Weibull distribution has a basis for utilization for fatigue analysis.

Albekis (1967) developed an alternative distribution for low probabilities of failure. Data have shown that the Weibull may be non-conservative for very low probabilities of failure (Fuchs and Stevens 1980). The selection of distributions for analysis must be carefully considered in anticipating probabilities of failure below about 0.1 .

# 5.4.2 S-N Diagrams for Components

As we have discussed, the manufacturing processes and component configuration will significantly effect the fatigue life. We can expect the following factors to significantly effect fatigue life, when a material is processed into a component:

- Surface condition
- Size
- Stress Concentration
- Temperature
- Stress State
- Environment

Each of these factors will reduce the fatigue strength of a material. Hence, we can modify our simple power model relating the fatigue strength, $S_{f}$ to the number of cycles to failure, incorporating a fatigue strength reduction factor for each item on our list that will affect our component, as shown in equation 5.17.


$$

S*{f}=C^{\*} \prod*{1}^{a} k*{a} \mid N*{f}^{b}

$$

Shigley and Mitchell (1983) suggest a method for calculation of correction factors for fatigue design of components. They suggest that each factor be applied to reduce the fatigue limit, $S_{e}^{\prime}$, determined from a rotating bending test using polished specimens, to determine the component fatigue limit, $S_{e^{\prime}}$


$$

S*{e}=k*{a} \bullet k*{b} \bullet k*{c} \bullet k*{d} \bullet k*{e} \bullet k*{f} \bullet S*{e}^{\prime}

$$

Where


$$

\begin{aligned}
& S*{e}=\text { Endurance limit of the component } \\
& S*{e}^{\prime}=\text { Endurance limit of rotating-beam specimen } \\
& k*{a}=\text { Surface factor } \\
& k*{b}=\text { Size factor } \\
& k*{c}=\text { Reliability factor } \\
& k*{d}=\text { Temperature factor } \\
& k*{e}=\text { Modifying factor for stress concentration } \\
& k*{f}=\text { Miscellaneous-effects factor }
\end{aligned}

$$

Each $k$ factor must be determined according to the manufacturing processes, component geometry and desired reliability. Surface condition is among the most important factors in fatigue. Reduction factors for fatigue limits for components vary according to process, surface roughness and notch sensitivity. As an example, $k_{a}$ will range from 0.2 for high strength steels to 0.5 for more ductile steels, for as forged components. # 6.2.2 Errors Due to Mesh

Even if the selection of elements is proper, unacceptable errors could still occur because of the meshing procedure for the object under analysis. As has been described earlier, each element is a divided region of the structure or geometry and the mesh is the total collection of the elements. It is not enough to only take care of the small regions. There are many global issues that need special attention, such as the correct way to put all the right elements together.

One of the most fundamental issues is the density of the mesh. If it is too coarse, the accuracy of the results will be in question. However, time and cost penalties will occur if the mesh is unnecessarily too fine. If the use of use the FEA tool is to be practical engineering design, not to perform an academic numerical analysis, an optimized mesh will reasonably ensure the accuracy of the final results, while requiring a reasonable amount of time to solve. Overly fine meshes, significantly increase the degrees of freedom ( $d o f$ ) in the model and the computational time becomes too long to be practical. It is the author's experience and observation that, in most engineering designs involving FEA work, designers often use very fine meshes, rather than a reasonable coarse mesh, as an assurance for accuracy at higher expenses.

Another reason for using finer mesh as common practice in engineering design is the auto-meshing capability available in commercial FEA packages. While auto-meshing is

In reality, only localized fine mesh is needed based on the rapid gradient changes of the variables to be modeled. Thus the auto-meshing should be used with great care.

### 6.3 Applications in Reliability Assessment

In this section, we discuss practical FEA design and development problems, encountered frequently. We will examine a specific problem for microelectronics-heat dissipation and thermo-mechanical stress evaluations for a GaAs power monolithic microwave integrated circuit or MMIC device. We will treat all quantities in this analysis as deterministic, in order for us to focus on the application of analysis procedures. The modeling object has been modified and simplified, due to proprietary data restrictions, but no generality of FEA application, for such a reliability assessment, is lost.Power MMIC devices differ from the small signal devices mainly in that they dissipate higher power, within several very tiny regions of current flow called channels. Understanding the thermal characteristics of MMIC devices is essential because temperature variations will influence the operation of the circuits in terms of performance parameters, such as gain and efficiency. High operating temperatures can also severely limit the lifetime of the devices, or even catastrophically damage the device. Thus, designing a thermal environment, so that normal device temperatures under bias are maintained at specified levels, is critical for a MMIC designer to produce both reliable and cost effective circuits.

The primary goal of MMIC thermal design is to provide a means by which the dissipated heat can be carried away. This requires a low thermal resistance between the heat generation channels and the heat sink, which is usually a high conductivity metallic carrier, to which the GaAs chip is attached by a high conductivity bonding material. In most cases, the highest channel temperature is required to be below $125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in order to avoid the risk of failure by thermal runaway and to provide adequate overall reliability. Generally, the larger (or thicker) the heat sink is, the lower the channel temperature will be. Over design of the heat sink is not recommended, because of penalties associated with weight, volume and cost.

There are many examples of dissimilar electrode cells in engineering practice. In microelectronic devices, gold wires bonded to aluminum bond pads form a potentially destructive couple. The Nernst equation is expressed as follows for a half cell oxidation reaction: $$ E=E^{\mathrm{o}}+\left(\frac{0.0257 \text { Volts }}{n}\right)\left(\frac{T}{298 K}\right) \ln \kappa $$ $n$ is the valance of the oxidized species, $T$ is the temperature in Kelvin and $\kappa$ is the chemical equilibrium constant. The equilibrium constant, $\kappa$, for any reaction is a function of the reacting species chemical activity. In general we write a reaction in its equilibrium state as: $$ a A+b B=c C+d D $$ Then $\kappa$ is expressed as: $$ \kappa=\frac{[\mathrm{C}]^{c}[\mathrm{D}]^{d}}{[\mathrm{~A}]^{a}[\mathrm{~B}]^{b}} $$ The value or magnitude of $\kappa$ is then indicative how far the reaction will progress to the right. The bracketed quantities are the activities for each species in the reaction. The chemical activity for a solid element is generally taken as 1 . However, the activity in an aqueous solution is equivalent to the molar concentration. For gaseous species, activity is taken as the partial pressure of the reacting component. In this case, we have handled the calculation in a deterministic fashion. We can apply Monte Carlo simulation to estimate the failure distribution. We require some knowledge of the distributions of the parameters in the time to failure equation.

Another form of evaluating corrosion in structures and components is based upon weight loss. A weight loss test is conducted and the results are projected as thickness loss, over the corroding area. Weight loss tests may be conducted under accelerated conditions, such as increased temperature. The results are then projected to service conditions. The corrosion penetration rate can be related from the weight loss rate in testing, using the following equation:

$$
\dot{p}=87.6 \frac{\dot{w}_{\text {test }}}{\rho A}
$$

In the expression shown, $\dot{p}$ is the corrosion penetration rate in mm per year, $\rho$ is the density in $\mathrm{gm} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$ and $A$ is the corroding area in $\mathrm{cm}^{2} . \dot{w}_{\text {test }}$ is the measured weight loss in milligrams per hour, under similar conditions to the environment expected in service. Considering a critical penetration depth, $h^{*}$ in mm, with a pitting factor, $P F$, we can express the time to failure for a component under corrosion, $t_{f}$, in years, as follows:

$$
t_{f}=\frac{h^{*}}{P F \cdot \dot{p}}=\frac{h^{*}}{P F} \cdot \frac{\rho A}{87.6 \dot{w}_{\text {test }}}
$$

While the units in these expressions may seem odd to the reader, they are generally the units of choice for testing and corrosion penetration rates (Fontana 1989, Uhlig 1971). Appropriate acceleration factors must be determined for tests at elevated temperatures.

# 7.3 Common Forms of Corrosion Attack

Fontana (1986) identifies eight forms of corrosion in which varies types of galvanic cells may be active. This classification is conveniently based upon the appearance of the corroded surfaces of the components. These eight forms will be briefly discussed in this section. In addition, a further discussion of corrosion in electronics may be found in Chapter 8. In addition to this classic description of the eight forms of corrosion, we can will also consider related mechanisms including stress sorption cracking of polymer materials, hydrogen embrittlement of steels and corrosion fatigue.

### 7.3.1 Eight Forms of Corrosion

The eight forms of corrosion identified by the Fontana classification include:

- Uniform Attack
- Galvanic Coupling
- Crevice Corrosion
- Pitting
- Intergranular Corrosion
- Parting
- Errosion Corrosion
- Stress Corrosion Cracking

## Uniform Attack

Uniform attack is the general and uniform loss of exposed metal surface. It is the most common form of corrosion. It is most easily characterized by the example of rust formation in the atmosphere on exposed iron or steel. This process generally involves most of the

For the mathematical formulation of the model, let the basic probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ be equipped with a filtration $\mathbb{F}$, the complete information level, to which all processes are adapted, and let $S=\{1, \ldots, m\}$ be the set of unobservable states. We assume that the time points of failures (minimal repairs) $0<T_{1}<T_{2}<\cdots$ form a Markov-modulated Poisson process as described in Example 3.14, p. 65. Let us recapitulate the details:

- The changes of the states are driven by a homogeneous Markov process $Y=\left(Y_{t}\right), t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$, with values in $S$ and infinitesimal parameters $q_{i}$, the rate to leave state $i$, and $q_{i j}$, the rate to reach state $j$ from state $i$

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{i} & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0+} \frac{1}{h} P\left(Y_{h} \neq i \mid Y_{0}=i\right) \\
q_{i j} & =\lim _{h \rightarrow 0+} \frac{1}{h} P\left(Y_{h}=j \mid Y_{0}=i\right), i, j \in S, i \neq j \\
q_{i i} & =-q_{i}=-\sum_{j \neq i} q_{i j}
\end{aligned}
$$

- The time points $\left(T_{n}\right)$ form a point process and $N=\left(N_{t}\right), t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$, is the corresponding counting process $N_{t}=\sum_{n \geq 1} I\left(T_{n} \leq t\right)$, which has a stochastic intensity $\lambda_{Y_{t}}$ depending on the unobservable state, i.e., $N$ admits the representation

$$
N_{t}=\int_{0}^{t} \lambda_{Y_{s}} d s+M_{t}
$$

where $M$ is an $\mathbb{F}$-martingale and $0<\lambda_{i}<\infty, i \in S$. Since the filtration $\mathbb{F}^{\lambda}\left(\mathbb{F}^{\lambda}=\mathbb{F}^{Y}\right.$, if $\lambda_{i} \neq \lambda_{j}$ for $\left.i \neq j\right)$ generated by the intensity does not include $\mathbb{F}^{N}$ as a subfiltration, it follows that $T_{n}, n \in \mathbb{N}$, is not an $\mathbb{F}^{\lambda_{-}}$ stopping time. Therefore, according to Definition 3.50, p. 92, $N$ is a MRP.

- $\left(X_{n}\right), n \in \mathbb{N}$, is a sequence of positive i.i.d. random variables, independent of $N$ and $Y$, with common distribution $F$ and finite mean $\mu$. The cost caused by the $n$th minimal repair at time $T_{n}$ is described by $X_{n}$.
- There is an initial capital $u$ and an income of constant rate $c>0$ per unit time.

Now the process $R$, given by

$$
R_{t}=u+c t-\sum_{n=1}^{N_{t}} X_{n}
$$

describes the available capital at time $t$ as the difference of the income and the total amount of costs for minimal repairs up to time $t$.The process $R$ is commonly used in other branches of applied probability like queueing or collective risk theory. In risk theory one is mainly interested in the distribution of the time to ruin $\tau=\inf \left\{t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}: R_{t} \leq 0\right\}$.

# The Failure Rate Process of the Ruin Time 

We want to show that the indicator process $V_{t}=I(\tau(u) \leq t)$ has a semimartingale representation

$$
V_{t}=I(\tau \leq t)=\int_{0}^{t} I(\tau>s) h_{s} d s+M_{t}, t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}
$$

where $M$ is a mean zero martingale with respect to the filtration $\mathbb{F}=\left(\mathcal{F}_{t}\right), t \in$ $\mathbb{R}_{+}$, which is generated by all introduced random quantities:

$$
\mathcal{F}_{t}=\sigma\left(N_{s}, Y_{s}, X_{i}, 0 \leq s \leq t, i=1, \ldots, N_{t}\right)
$$

The failure rate process $h=\left(h_{t}\right), t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$, can be derived in the same way as was done for shock models with failures of threshold type (cf. p. 89). Note that ruin can only occur at a failure time; therefore, the ruin time is a hitting time of a compound point process:

$$
\tau=\inf \left\{t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}: A_{t}=\sum_{n=1}^{N_{t}} B_{n} \geq u\right\}=\inf \left\{T_{n}: A_{T_{n}} \geq u\right\}
$$

where $B_{n}=X_{n}-c U_{n}$ and $U_{n}=T_{n}-T_{n-1}, n=1,2, \ldots$. Replacing $X_{t}$ by $A_{t}$, $r\left(t-T_{n}\right)$ by $\lambda_{Y_{t}}$, and the threshold $S$ by $u$ in formula (3.20) on p. 90, we get the following lemma.

Lemma 3.56. Let $\tau=\tau(u)$ be the ruin time and $F$ the distribution of the claim sizes, $\bar{F}(x)=F((x, \infty))=P\left(X_{1}>x\right), x \in \mathbb{R}$. Then the $\mathbb{F}$-failure rate process $h$ is given by

$$
h_{t}=\lambda_{Y_{t}} \bar{F}\left(R_{t}-\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{m} \lambda_{i} I\left(Y_{t}=i\right) \bar{F}\left(R_{t}-\right), t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}
$$

The failure rate processes $h$ is bounded above by $\max \left\{\lambda_{i}: i \in S\right\}$. If all claim arrival rates $\lambda_{i}$ coincide, $\lambda=\lambda_{i}, i \in S$, we have the classical Poisson case, and it is not surprising that the hazard rate decreases when the risk reserve increases and vice versa. Of course, the paths of $R$ are not monotone and so the failure rate processes do not have monotone paths either. But they have (stochastically) a tendency to increase or decrease in the following sense. As follows from the results of Sect. 3.3.3 the process $R$ has an $\mathbb{F}$-semimartingale representation

$$
R_{t}=\int_{0}^{t} \sum_{i=1}^{m} I\left(Y_{s}=i\right)\left(c-\lambda_{i} \mu\right) d s+L_{t}
$$with a mean zero $\mathbb{F}$-martingale $L$. If we have positive drift in all environmental states, i.e., $c-\lambda_{i} \mu>0, i=1, \ldots, m$, then $R$ is a submartingale and it is seen that $h$ tends to 0 as $t \rightarrow \infty$ ( $P$-a.s.). On the other hand, if the claim rate $\lambda_{Y_{t}}$ is increasing ( $P$-a.s.) and the drift is nonpositive for all states, i.e., $c-\lambda_{i} \mu \leq$ $0, i=1, \ldots, m$, and $\bar{F}$ is convex on the support of the distribution, then $R$ is a supermartingale and it follows by Jensen's inequality for conditional expectations:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E\left[h_{t+s} \mid \mathcal{F}_{t}\right] & =E\left[\lambda_{Y_{t+s}} \bar{F}\left(R_{t+s}-\right) \mid \mathcal{F}_{t}\right] \geq E\left[\lambda_{Y_{t}} \bar{F}\left(R_{t+s}-\right) \mid \mathcal{F}_{t}\right] \\
& =\lambda_{Y_{t}} E\left[\bar{F}\left(R_{t+s}-\right) \mid \mathcal{F}_{t}\right] \geq \lambda_{Y_{t}} \bar{F}\left(E\left[R_{t+s}-\mid \mathcal{F}_{t}\right]\right) \\
& \geq \lambda_{Y_{t}} \bar{F}\left(R_{t}-\right)=h_{t}, t, s \in \mathbb{R}_{+}
\end{aligned}
$$

This shows that $h$ is a submartingale, i.e., $h$ is stochastically increasing.

# Bounds for Finite Time Ruin Probabilities 

Except in simple cases, such as Poisson arrivals of exponentially distributed claims ( $\mathrm{P} / \mathrm{E}$ case), the finite time ruin probabilities $\psi(u, t)=P(\tau(u) \leq t)$ cannot be expressed by the basic model parameters in an explicit form. So there is a variety of suggested bounds and approximations (see Asmussen [9] and Grandell [78] for overviews). In the following, bounds for the ruin probabilities in finite time will be derived that are based on the semimartingale representation given in Lemma 3.56. It turns out that especially for small values of $t$ known bounds can be improved.

From now on we assume that the claim arrival process is Poisson with rate $\lambda>0$. Then Lemma 3.56 yields the representation

$$
V_{t}=I(\tau(u) \leq t)=\int_{0}^{t} I(\tau(u)>s) \lambda \bar{F}\left(R_{s}\right) d s+M_{t}, t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}
$$

Note that the paths of $R$ have only countable numbers of jumps such that under the integral sign $R_{s}-$ can be replaced by $R_{s}$. Taking expectations on both sides of (3.24) one gets by Fubini's theorem

$$
\begin{aligned}
\psi(u, t) & =\int_{0}^{t} E\left[I(\tau(u)>s) \lambda \bar{F}\left(R_{s}\right)\right] d s \\
& =\int_{0}^{t}(1-\psi(u, s)) \lambda E\left[\bar{F}\left(R_{s}\right) \mid \tau(u)>s\right] d s
\end{aligned}
$$

As a solution of this integral equation we have the following representation of the finite time ruin probability:

$$
\psi(u, t)=1-\exp \left\{-\int_{0}^{t} \lambda E\left[\bar{F}\left(R_{s}\right) \mid \tau(u)>s\right] d s\right\}
$$

This shows that the (possibly defective) distribution of $\tau(u)$ has the hazard rate

$$
\lambda E\left[\bar{F}\left(R_{t}\right) \mid \tau(u)>t\right]
$$Now let $N^{X}$ be the renewal process generated by the sequence $\left(X_{i}\right), i \in \mathbb{N}$, $N_{t}^{X}=\sup \left\{k \in \mathbb{N}_{0}: \sum_{i=1}^{k} X_{i} \leq t\right\}$, and $A(u, t)=\int_{0}^{t} a(u, s) d s$, where $a(u, s)=\lambda P\left(N_{u+c s}^{X}=N_{s}\right)$. Then bounds for $\psi(u, t)$ can be established.

Theorem 3.57. For all $u, t \geq 0$, the following inequality holds true:

$$
B(u, t) \leq \psi(u, t) \leq A(u, t)
$$

where $A$ is defined as above and $B(u, t)=1-\exp \left\{-\lambda \int_{0}^{t} \bar{F}(u+c s) d s\right\}$.
Proof. For the lower bound we use the representation (3.26) and simply observe that $E\left[\bar{F}\left(R_{s}\right) \mid \tau(u)>s\right] \geq \bar{F}(u+c s)$.

For the upper bound we start with formula (3.24). Since $\{\tau(u)>t\} \subset$ $\left\{R_{t} \geq 0\right\}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{t} & =\int_{0}^{t} I(\tau(u)>s) \lambda \bar{F}\left(R_{s}\right) d s+M_{t} \\
& \leq \int_{0}^{t} I\left(R_{s} \geq 0\right) \lambda \bar{F}\left(R_{s}\right) d s+M_{t}
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking expectations on both sides of this inequality we get

$$
\psi(u, t)=E V_{t} \leq \int_{0}^{t} \lambda E\left[I\left(R_{s} \geq 0\right) \bar{F}\left(R_{s}\right)\right] d s
$$

It remains to show that $a(u, t)=\lambda E\left[I\left(R_{s} \geq 0\right) \bar{F}\left(R_{s}\right)\right]$. Denoting the $k$-fold convolution of $F$ by $F^{* k}$ and $T_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} X_{i}$ it follows by the independence of the claim arrival process and $\left(X_{i}\right), i \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E & {\left[I\left(R_{t} \geq 0\right) \bar{F}\left(u+c t-\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t}} X_{i}\right)\right] } \\
& =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} E\left[I\left(u+c t-\sum_{i=1}^{k} X_{i} \geq 0\right) \bar{F}\left(u+c t-\sum_{i=1}^{k} X_{i}\right)\right] P\left(N_{t}=k\right) \\
& =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{u+c t} \bar{F}(u+c t-x) d F^{* k}(x) P\left(N_{t}=k\right) \\
& =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\left\{F^{* k}(u+c t)-F^{*(k+1)}(u+c t)\right\} P\left(N_{t}=k\right) \\
& =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} P\left(N_{u+c t}^{X}=k\right) P\left(N_{t}=k\right) \\
& =P\left(N_{u+c t}^{X}=N_{t}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

In this chapter we combine the general lifetime model of Chap. 3 with maintenance actions like repairs and replacements. Given a certain cost and reward structure an optimal repair and replacement strategy will be derived. We begin with some basic and well-known models and come then to more complex ones, which show how the general approach can be exploited to open a variety of different optimization models.

### 5.1 Basic Replacement Models

First of all we consider some basic models that are simple in both the lifetime modeling and the optimization criterion. These basic models include the age and the block replacement models that are widely used and thoroughly investigated. A technical system is considered, the lifetime of which is described by a positive random variable $T$ with distribution $F$. Upon failure the system is immediately replaced by an equivalent one and the process repeats itself. A preventive replacement can be carried out before failure. Each replacement incurs a cost of $c>0$ and each failure adds a penalty cost $k>0$.

### 5.1.1 Age Replacement Policy

For this policy a replacement age $s, s>0$, is fixed for each system at which a preventive replacement takes place. If $T_{i}, i=1,2, \ldots$, are the successive lifetimes of the systems, then $\tau_{i}=T_{i} \wedge s$ denotes the operating time of the $i$ th system and equals the $i$ th cycle length. The random variables $T_{i}$ are assumed to form an i.i.d. sequence with common distribution $F$, i.e., $F(t)=P\left(T_{i} \leq t\right)$. The costs for one cycle are described by the stochastic process $Z=\left(Z_{t}\right), t \in$ $\mathbb{R}_{+}, Z_{t}=c+k I(T \leq t)$. Clearly, the average cost after $n$ cycles is$$
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_{\tau_{i}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_{i}}
$$

and the total cost per unit time up to time $t$ is given by

$$
C_{t}=\frac{1}{t} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{t}} Z_{\tau_{i}}
$$

where $\left(N_{t}\right), t \in \mathbb{R}_{+}$, is the renewal counting process generated by $\left(\tau_{i}\right)$ and $Z_{\tau}=c+k I(T \leq \tau)$ describes the incurred costs in one cycle. It is well known from renewal theory (see Appendix B, p. 280) that the limits of the expectations of these ratios, $K_{s}$, coincide and are equal to the ratio of the expected costs for one cycle and the expected cycle length:

$$
K_{s}=\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} E\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_{\tau_{i}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_{i}}\right]=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} E C_{t}=\frac{E Z_{\tau}}{E \tau}
$$

The objective is to find the replacement age that minimizes this long run average cost per unit time. Inserting the cost function $Z_{t}=c+k I(T \leq t)$ we get

$$
K_{s}=\frac{c+k F(s)}{\int_{0}^{s}(1-F(x)) d x}
$$

Now elementary analysis can be used to find the optimal replacement age $s$, i.e., to find $s^{*}$ with

$$
K_{s^{*}}=\inf \left\{K_{s}: s \in \mathbb{R}_{+} \cup\{\infty\}\right\}
$$

Here $s^{*}=\infty$ means that preventive replacements do not pay and it is optimal to replace only at failures. As can be easily seen this case occurs if the lifetimes are exponentially distributed, i.e., if $F(t)=1-\exp \{-\lambda t\}, t \geq 0, \lambda>0$, then $K_{\infty}=\lambda(c+k) \leq K_{s}$ for all $s>0$.

# Maintainability 

When a system fails to perform satisfactorily, repair is normally carried out to locate and correct the fault. The system is restored to operational effectiveness by making an adjustment or by replacing a component.

Maintainability is defined as the probability that a failed system will be restored to specified conditions within a given period of time when maintenance is performed according to prescribed procedures and resources. In other words, maintainability is the probability of isolating and repairing a fault in a system within a given time. Maintainability engineers must work with system designers to ensure that the system product can be maintained by the customer efficiently and cost effectively. This function requires the analysis of part removal, replacement, tear-down, and build-up of the product in order to determine the required time to carry out the operation, the necessary skill, the type of support equipment and the documentation.

Let $T$ denote the random variable of the time to repair or the total downtime. If the repair time $T$ has a repair time density function $g(t)$, then the maintainability, $V(t)$, is defined as the probability that the failed system will be back in service by time $t$, i.e.,

$$
V(t)=P(T \leq t)=\int_{0}^{t} g(s) d s
$$

For example, if $g(t)=\mu e^{-\mu t}$ where $\mu>0$ is a constant repair rate, then

$$
V(t)=1-e^{-\mu t}
$$

which represents the exponential form of the maintainability function.
