# 12.4.2 Statement of the Problem 

The tubes are placed vertically in the furnace. The tubes have an internal diameter of 5.00 in., a wall thickness of 0.4 in., and a length of 45 ft . The design temperature of the tubes is $1710^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$ and the design internal pressure is 400 psi (pounds per square inch). The tubes are flanged at the top end with a reduced diameter at the bottom end that leads into a smaller tube (common to a set of 15 tubes), which in turn feeds into an outlet collection header.

The expected design life of the tubes when the furnace operates at the normal operating conditions is 100000 hours. This design life is calculated based on the Larson-Miller design formula, which relates the properties of the tube material to the operating temperature and pressure. The formula is empirically developed.

Increasing the oil production requires an increase in the hydrogen production, which in turn increases the furnace burner rate. As a result, the temperature in the furnace tends to increase, which causes a significant reduction in the remaining life of the tubes. Analysis of failure data collected over 8 years of operation shows that operating a tube at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$ above the design temperature of $1710^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$ results in a loss of one-half of the tube's remaining life. Temperature readings taken by an optical pyrometer show that approximately 5 out of 15 tubes within the same set operate at temperatures of $1724^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$.

The furnace fails when four out of 15 tubes fail or when two consecutive tubes fail. The engineers of the oil company are interested in estimating the reliability of the furnace and the remaining life of each set of tubes. The furnace has 10 sets of tubes and all are required for the proper function of the furnace. The engineers are also interested in determining the optimal preventive maintenance schedule that minimizes the downtime of the furnace.

The manufacturer of the tubes performs an accelerated life testing at $1835^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$ on 25 tubes and records the following failure times:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 1958,1013,12416,755,2901,7225,511,2044,191,8034,6038,886,1441 \\
& 11479,734,327,1986,6701,12822,3090,3521,1292,1245,8106,8163
\end{aligned}
$$

A $25^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$ increase in the operating temperature of the furnace results in a $10 \%$ increase in the number of oil barrels produced. The net profit per barrel is $\$ 20$, and the cost of replacing allthe tubes is $\$ 15$ million and requires 1 year. What is the operating temperature, above the design temperature that maximizes the profit? It should be noted that the furnace cannot operate beyond $1810^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$.

# 12.4.3 Solution 

We first test the validity of using a constant failure rate model by calculating the Bartlett value, $B_{r}$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{25} \ln t_{i} & =194.38 \\
T & =\sum_{i=1}^{n} t_{i}=104879
\end{aligned}
$$

Using Equation 5.2, we obtain

$$
B_{r}=\frac{2 \times 25\left[\ln \left(\frac{104879}{25}\right)-\frac{1}{25} \times 194.38\right]}{1+(26) /(6 \times 25)}=24.14
$$

The critical values for a two-tailed test with $\alpha=0.10$ are

$$
\chi_{0.95,24}^{2}=13.8484 \quad \text { and } \quad \chi_{0.05,24}^{2}=36.4151
$$

Therefore, $B_{25}$ does not contradict the hypothesis that the failure times can be modeled by an exponential distribution.

The failure rate at the stress level of $1835^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$ is

$$
\lambda_{1835 \mathrm{~F}}=\frac{25}{104879}=2.3837 \times 10^{-4} \text { failures } / \mathrm{h}
$$

Since operating the furnace at $25^{\circ} \mathrm{F}$ above the design temperature results in a loss of onehalf the remaining life of the tubes, the acceleration factor between the design temperature $\left(1710^{\circ} \mathrm{F}\right)$ and the accelerated test temperature $\left(1835^{\circ} \mathrm{F}\right)$ is 25 , and

$$
\lambda_{1710^{\circ} \mathrm{F}}=9.53 \times 10^{-6} \text { failures } / \mathrm{h}
$$

The reliability of a single tube is

$$
R(t)=e^{-9.53 \times 10^{-6} t}
$$

The p.d.f. of the failure time of a single tube is

$$
f(t)=\frac{-d R(t)}{d t}=9.53 \times 10^{-6} e^{-9.53 \times 10^{-6} t}
$$

The mean life at the normal conditions is $1 / \lambda=104931$ hours.
If we assume that the tubes have been operating for five years ( 50000 hours), then the residual life of a tube is obtained using Equation 1.113$$
\begin{aligned}
L(t) & =\frac{1}{R(t)} \int_{t}^{\infty} \tau f(\tau) d \tau-t \\
L(50000) & =\frac{1}{R(50000)} \int_{50000}^{\infty} 9.53 \times 10^{-6} t e^{-9.53 \times 10^{-6} t} d t-50000
\end{aligned}
$$

or

$$
L(50000)=\frac{1}{\lambda}=104931 \text { hours. }
$$

Since the exponential distribution has a memoryless property, the remaining life at any time $t$ is always $1 / \lambda$.

The reliability of a set of 15 tubes is obtained by examining the two possible failure modes: (i) 4-out-of-15 tubes fail system or (ii) consecutive-2-out-of-15 F system.

Reliability of the 4 -out-of-15 system is

$$
R_{a}(t)=\sum_{r=11}^{15}\binom{15}{r}\left(e^{-\lambda t}\right)^{r}\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)^{15-r}
$$

or

$$
\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}
$$

or

\begin{aligned}
R_{a}(t)= & 1365 e^{-10.483 \times 10^{-5} t}-5005 e^{-11.436 \times 10^{-5} t}+6930 e^{-12.389 \times 10^{-5} t} \\
& -4290 e^{-13.342 \times 10^{5} t}+1001 e^{-14.295 \times 10^{-5} t}
\end{aligned}
$$

Reliability of a consecutive-2-out-of-15 $F$ system is obtained using Equation 2.15 as

R_{b}(p, 2, n)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor(n+1) / 2\rfloor}\binom{n-j+1}{j}(1-p)^{j} p^{n-j}
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}

= & 0.5 e^{-6.671 \times 10^{-5} t}+14 e^{-7.624 \times 10^{-5} t}-7 e^{-8.577 \times 10^{-5} t} \\

12.4.3.2 Preventive Maintenance Let $c_{1}$ be the cost per inspection for a tube and $c_{2}$ the cost of an undetected failure, then the optimum inspection interval, $T$, that minimizes the total expected cost per unit time is the value of $T^{*}$ which minimizes Equation 10.92 or

$$
c(t)=\frac{c_{1}+c_{2} T}{1-e^{-\lambda T}}-\frac{c_{2}}{\lambda}
$$

From Figure 12.9, the failure rate of a set of tubes is $\lambda=8.45 \times 10^{-5}$ failures $/ \mathrm{h}$.
Assume $c_{2}=\$ 900$ and $c_{1}=\$ 1200$. Then

$$
c\left(T^{*}\right)=\frac{1200+900 T^{*}}{1-e^{-8.45 \times 10^{-5}}}-\frac{900}{8.45 \times 10^{-5}}
$$

and

$$
T^{*}=178 \text { hours. }
$$

In other words, every set of tubes should be inspected after 178 hours of operation.

# 12.8 CASE 8: SYSTEM DESIGN USING RELIABILITY OBJECTIVES* 

### 12.8.1 Introduction

Telecommunications service continuity is controlled by availability design objectives applicable to networks, network segments, and network elements. In general, these objectives are intended to control the amount of time that networks or portions of networks are unable to perform their required function. Availability objectives are typically stated as a single number equal to the long-term percentage of time that a system is expected to provide service. (System is a generic term used to describe an entity to which availability objectives apply. This could be a network, a network segment, or a network element.) As such, these objectives can significantly influence end-user perception of service quality.

This case discusses some of the implications of using traditional availability design objectives to control performance. This is done by first considering how current availability objectives apply to the design of a single system, and then by examining the resulting availability service performance across a population of systems, each of which is designed to meet the same availability design objective. New methods for describing end-user availability performance are discussed, and how they can be used to (i) evaluate current network and service objectives, (ii) aid in the development of a top-down approach to setting availability objectives for new services, and (iii) provide better network performance quality control.

The topics discussed in this case are addressed because there continue to be questions about the interpretation of availability design objectives for new services and supporting technologies. Two such questions are as follows.

- An objective for total downtime of a common control Bell System switching system was first established in the late 1950s, and evolved during the 1960s. The resulting objective required that there be "no more than two hours total downtime in 40 years." The same objective is used today and is stated as a downtime objective of three minutes per year for current switching systems. If a switching system is down for more than three minutes in a year, has it failed to meet its design objective?
- If, after a period of several years, there are switching systems in a given population that have experienced (i) no downtime, and/or (ii) downtime less than the objective, and/or (iii) downtime greater than the objective, has the system design objective been met?

As we shall discuss, the answer to the first question is "not necessarily." The answer to the second question is that we interpret the design objective as having been met if the average of the population downtime distribution does not exceed the objective value.

# B. 3 Estimating Field Failures 

Suppose a product has a 1,000-hour system MTBF. Then $\lambda$ will be $1 / 1,000$ or 0.001 . This means that every 1,000 hours a system will have a failure. With 100 systems then there will be 100 failures in those 1,000 hours. Remember that these failures will show up in only 63 units; the other 37 units will exhibit no failures during this time period.
So how many of the 63 units had $1,2,3, \ldots$ or $n$ failures?
The number of units having more than one failure can be determined using:

$$
P(n)=\left[\left(\lambda^{n} \times t^{n}\right) / n!\right] \times \varepsilon^{-\lambda t}
$$

where:
$P(n)$ is the percent of units exhibiting $n$ failures.
$t$ is the time duration,
$n$ is the number of failures in a single system, (e.g. 1, 2, 3, $\ldots n$ ).
Let's learn how many units will have 1 , then 2 , then 3 , and so on, failures per unit in the group of 63 units that will exhibit these 100 failures.
But first a short refresher in factorials:
Note: 0 ! is defined as equaling 1 ; and 0 ! is read as "zero factorial." See Table B. 2 for a list of common factorials.
For zero failures: (This is the group of 37 units that had no failures in 1,000 hours.)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P(0)=\left[\left(0.001^{0} \times 1,000^{0}\right) / 1\right] \times 2.71^{-(0.001 \times 1,000)} \\
& =[(1 \times 1)] / 1 \times 2.71^{-1} \\
& =1 \times 0.37 \\
& P(0)=0.37 \text { or } 37 \%
\end{aligned}
$$

So with 100 units there will be 37 units exhibiting zero failures in one MTBF time period.
How many units will have one failure in 1,000 hours?
Substitute 1 for $n$ :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P(1)=\left[\left(0.001^{1} \times 1,000^{1}\right) / 1\right] \times 2.71^{-1} \\
& P(1)=(1 / 1) \times 0.37 \\
& P(1)=0.37, \text { or } 37 \% \text { will exhibit one failure. }
\end{aligned}
$$

So with 100 units, there will be 37 units exhibiting one failure in one MTBF time period ( 1,000 hours).
How many units will have two failures in 1,000 hours?

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P(2)=\left[\left(0.001^{2} \times 1,000^{2}\right) / 2\right] \times 0.37 \\
& P(2)=(1 / 2) \times 0.37 \\
& P(2)=18 \%
\end{aligned}

Find how many will fail in one-hundredth of an MTBF time period.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& P(f)=0.001 \times 1,000 / 100 \mathrm{~h} \\
& P(f)=0.001 \times 10 \\
& P(f)=0.01 \text { or } 1 \%
\end{aligned}
$$

Using 100 units, this means that 1 unit exhibits the very first failure in 10 hours. So the time to first failure is 10 hours!!!

Which one it will be in the 100 units is a mystery, however ....
Interestingly enough, 1 unit will last for 5,000 hours before it finally has its first failure.
Note: These failures have been considered where the failure rate was exponential. There are other failure rates that are Weibull, lognormal, and more.

# B.3.1 Comparing Repairable to Nonrepairable Systems 

If the system is comprised of nonrepairable systems, the number of failures in one MTBF period is lower.

In repairable systems, when a unit fails it is quickly repaired and placed back into service. If the unit cannot be repaired, then when 1 unit fails in 100 systems, there will be 99 units operating after the first failure. Then 98,97 , and so on until they all eventually fail. In 100 systems that are nonrepairable, there will be 67 units that will fail in one MTBF time period. If the MTBF were 10,000 hours, then two MTBFs would be 20,000 hours. In applications with high reliability, availability or safety requirements, items must be designed to be fault tolerant at components level and/or fault tolerant reconfigurable at equipment \& systems level (see e.g. pp.49, 65 \& [2.36,4.4,4.26,5.77]). Methods to investigate fault tolerant items have been introduced in Sections 2.2.6.2 through 2.3.6, in particular Sections 2.2.6.5 (majority redundancy) and 2.3.6 (quad redundancy). The latter is one of the few structures which can support at least one failure of any mode, the price paid is four devices instead of one. Other possibilities are known to implement fault tolerance at components level, e. g. [2.41].

Repairable fault tolerant reconfigurable systems are considered carefully in Chapter 6, in particular Sections 6.8 - 6.11 (pp. 238 - 310). It is shown, that the stochastic processes introduced in Appendix A7 are useful to investigate reliability and availability of fault tolerant systems also if a reliability block diagram does not exist. However, for repairable and nonrepairable systems,
to avoid common cause or single-point failures, redundant elements of fault tolerant equipment and systems must be designed and realized independently from each other, in critical cases with different technologies, tools, and personnel (in particular for software); also mandatory is the investigation of all possible failure (fault) modes, using FMEA/ FMECA, FTA, causes-to-effects diagrams, or similar tools (Sections 2.6 \& 6.9).

Failure modes analysis is essential where redundancy appears, among other to identify parts which are in series to the ideal redundancy (in the reliability block diagram), to discover interactions between elements or modules, and to find appropriate measures to avoid failure propagation (secondary failures). Protection against secondary failures can be realized at component level with decoupling elements such as diodes (Example 2.3 on p. 32), resistors, capacitors. ## Example 2.16

Let the strength $\xi_{S}$ of a rod be normally distributed with mean $m_{S}=450 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}-$ $0.01 t \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$ and standard deviation $\sigma_{S}=25 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}+0.001 t \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$. The stress $\xi_{L}$ is constant and equal $350 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$. Calculate the reliability of the rod at $t=0$ and $t=10^{4} \mathrm{~h}$.

## Solution

At $t=0, m_{S}=450 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \& \sigma_{S}=25 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$, and the reliability is

$$
R_{S 0}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{S}>\xi_{L}\right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{\frac{350-450}{25}}^{\infty} e^{-y^{2} / 2} d y \approx 0.99997
$$

After 10,000 operating hours, $m_{S}=350 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2} \& \sigma_{S}=35 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$, and the reliability is

$$
R_{S 0}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{S}>\xi_{L}\right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{\frac{350-350}{35}}^{\infty} e^{-y^{2} / 2} d y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-y^{2} / 2} d y=0.5
$$Equation (2.76) holds for a one-item structure. For a series model, i. e. in particular for the series connection of two independent elements one obtains:

1. Same stress $\xi_{L}\left(\xi_{L}, \xi_{S_{i}}>0\right)$

$$
R_{S 0}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{S_{1}}>\xi_{L} \cap \xi_{S_{2}}>\xi_{L}\right\}=\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}_{L}(x)\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{S_{1}}(x)\right)\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{S_{2}}(x)\right) d x
$$

2. Independent stresses $\xi_{L_{1}}$ and $\xi_{L_{2}}\left(\xi_{L_{i}}, \xi_{S_{i}}>0\right)$

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_{S 0} & =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{S_{1}}>\xi_{L_{1}} \cap \xi_{S_{2}}>\xi_{L_{2}}\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{S_{1}}>\xi_{L_{1}}\right\} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{S_{2}}>\xi_{L_{2}}\right\} \\
& =\left(\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}_{L_{1}}(x)\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{S_{1}}(x)\right) d x\right)\left(\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}_{L_{2}}(x)\left(1-\mathrm{F}_{S_{2}}(x)\right) d x\right) \doteq R_{1} R_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

For a parallel model, i.e. in particular for the parallel connection of two non repairable independent elements it follows that:

1. Same stress $\xi_{L}\left(\xi_{L}, \xi_{S_{i}}>0\right)$

$$
R_{S 0}=1-\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{S_{1}} \leq \xi_{L} \cap \xi_{S_{2}} \leq \xi_{L}\right\}=1-\int_{0}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}_{L}(x) \mathrm{F}_{S_{1}}(x) \mathrm{F}_{S_{2}}(x) d x
$$

2. Independent stresses $\xi_{L_{1}}$ and $\xi_{L_{2}}\left(\xi_{L_{i}}, \xi_{S_{i}}>0\right)$

$$
R_{S 0}=1-\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{S_{1}} \leq \xi_{L_{1}}\right\} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{S_{2}} \leq \xi_{L_{2}}\right\} \doteq 1-\left(1-R_{1}\right)\left(1-R_{2}\right)=R_{1}+R_{2}-R_{1} R_{2}
$$

As with Eqs. (2.78) and (2.80), the results of Table 2.1 (p.31) can be applied in the case of independent stresses and elements. However, this ideal situation is seldom true for mechanical systems, for which Eqs. (2.77) and (2.79) are often more realistic. Moreover, the uncertainty about the exact form of the distributions for stress and strength far from the mean value, severely reduce the accuracy of the results obtained from the above equations in practical applications (see also the footnote on p. 69). For mechanical items, tests and design of experiments (see e. g. [2.67]) are often the only way to evaluate their reliability. Investigations into new methods are in progress, paying particular attention to
the dependence between stresses and to a realistic truncation of the stress and strength distribution functions (as per Eq. (A6.33) or (A6.33a), using mixture of distribution functions (p. 444), or as a combination of both).

Other approaches are possible for mechanical items (systems), see e.g. [2.61-2.79].
For electronic items, Eqs. (2.76) and (2.77) - (2.80) can often be used to investigate drift failures. Quite generally, all considerations of Section 2.5 could be applied to electronic items. However, the method based on the failure rate, introduced in Section 2.2, is easier to be used and works reasonably well in many practical applications dealing with electronic and electromechanical equipment and systems.# 2.6 Failure Modes Analyses 

Failure rate analyses (Sections 2.1-2.5) basically do not account for the effect (consequence) of a failure. To understand the mechanism of system failures and in order to identify potential weaknesses of a fail-safe concept or a fail-safe procedure, it is necessary to perform a failure modes and effects analysis, at least where redundancy appears and for critical parts of the item considered. Such an analysis is termed FMEA (Failure Modes and Effects Analysis) or FMECA (Failure Modes, Effects, and Criticality Analysis) if also the failure severity is of interest. If failures and defects have to be considered, fault modes should be used, allowing errors/ flaws as possible causes as well.

An FMEA/FMECA consists of the systematic analysis of failure (fault) modes, their causes, effects (consequences), and criticality [2.80, 2.81, 2.83, 2.84, 2.86-2.93, 2.96-2.99], including common mode \& common cause as well. For critical applications (e.g. safety related), all parts of the item considered (one after the other) are investigated, in one run or in several steps (design FMEA/FMECA, process FMEA/ FMECA); see e.g. Tables 3.4 \& A10.1 and Section 3.3 for some considerations on failure modes of electronic components. Possibilities to avoid failures (faults) or to minimize (mitigate) their consequence must be analyzed and corresponding corrective (or preventive) actions have to be realized. The criticality describes the severity of the consequence of a failure (fault) and is designated by categories or levels which are function of the risk for damage or performance loss (Fig. 2.13).

The FMEA/FMECA is a bottom-up (inductive) procedure, performed as a teamwork with designer \& reliability engineers. The procedure is established in international standards [2.89]. It is easy to understand but can become time-consuming for complex equipment and systems. ### 4.5.1 Centralized Logistic Support, Nonrepairable Spare Parts

In centralized logistic support, spare parts are stocked at one place. The basic problem can be formulated as follows,at time $t=0$, the first part is put into operation, it fails at time $t=\tau_{1}$ and is replaced (in a negligible time) by a second part which fails at time $t=\tau_{1}+\tau_{2}$ and so forth; asked is the number $n$ of parts which must be stocked in order that the requirement for parts during the cumulative operating time $T$ is met with a given (fixed) probability $\gamma$.

To answer this question, the smallest integer $n$ must be found for which

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}>T\right\} \geq \gamma
$$

holds. In general, $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$ are assumed to be independent positive random variables with the same distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x)(\mathrm{F}(0)=0$, density $\mathrm{f}(x)) \&$ finite mean $\mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{i}\right]=\mathrm{E}[\tau]=$ MTTF $\& \operatorname{Var}\left[\tau_{i}\right]=\operatorname{Var}[\tau]$. If the number of parts is calculated from

$$
n=T / M T T F
$$

the requirement can only be covered (for $T$ large) with a probability of 0.5 . Thus, more than $T / M T T F$ parts are necessary to meet the requirement with $\gamma>0.5$.

According to Eq. (A7.12), valid for renewal processes, the probability as per Eq. (4.9) can be expressed by the $(n-1)$ th convolution of the distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ with itself, i. e.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{1}+\ldots+\tau_{n}>T\right\}=1-\mathrm{F}_{n}(T) \\
& \text { with } \quad \mathrm{F}_{1}(T)=\mathrm{F}(T) \quad \text { and } \quad \mathrm{F}_{n}(T)=\int_{0}^{T} \mathrm{~F}_{n-1}(T-x) \mathrm{f}(x) d x, \quad n>1
\end{aligned}
$$

Of the distribution functions $\mathrm{F}(x)$ used in reliability theory, a closed, simple form for the function $\mathrm{F}_{n}(x)$ exists only for the exponential, gamma, and normal distribution functions, yielding a Poisson, gamma, and normal distribution, respectively. In particular, the exponential distribution $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$ leads to (Eq. (A7.39))

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_{i}>T\right\}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \frac{(\lambda T)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda T}
$$

The important case of the Weibull distribution $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-(\lambda x)^{\beta}}$ must be solved numerically. Figure 4.3 shows the results with $\gamma$ and $\beta$ as parameters [4.2 (1974)].

For $n$ large, approximate solutions for a wide class of distribution functions $\mathrm{F}(x)$ can be obtained using the central limit theorem (Eq.(A6.148); $\mathrm{E}[\tau], \operatorname{Var}[\tau]<\infty$ ). ${ }^{*}$ )

$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\tau_{i}-\mathrm{E}[\tau]}{\sqrt{n \operatorname{Var}[\tau]}}>x\right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{x}^{\infty} e^{-y^{2} / 2} d y=1-\Phi(x)=\Phi(-x)
$$

and thus, using $x \sqrt{n \operatorname{Var}[\tau]}+n \mathrm{E}[\tau]=T$,

### 4.5.3 Repairable Spare Parts

In Sections $4.5 .1 \& 4.5 .2$ it was assumed that spare parts (e.g. LRUs) were nonrepairable. In many cases, spare parts can be repaired and stored for reuse. Calculation of the number of spare parts can be performed in a way similar to the investigation of a $k$-out-of-n standby redundancy, where $k$ is the number of parts used in the system and $n$ is the smallest integer to be determined such that the requirement is met with a given probability $\gamma$. Following two cases have to be considered:1. $\gamma$ is the probability that a request for a spare part at a time point $t$ can be met without time delay; in this case, $\gamma$ can be considered as the point availability $P A_{S}$ (in steady-state to simplify investigations) and $n$ is the smallest integer such that $P A_{S} \geq \gamma$ for a given (fixed) $\gamma$.
2. $\gamma$ is the probability that any request for a spare part during the time interval $(0, t]$ will be met without time delay; in this case, $\gamma$ can be considered as the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ ( $n$ as for Case 1 above but referred to $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \geq \gamma$ ).
If the spare parts have constant failure rate $\lambda=1 /$ MTTF and constant repair rate $\mu=1 / M T T R$, birth-and-death processes can be used (Appendix A7.5.5).*) To simplify investigations and to agree with results in Chapter 6, it is assumed that only one spare part at a time can be repaired (only 1 repair crew is available) and no further failures are considered when a request for a spare part cannot be met (corresponds to the assumption no further failure at system down (Fig. 6.13)).

For Case 1 above, Eq. (6.138) with $\lambda_{r} \cong 0$ and Eq. (6.140) yield

$$
P A_{S}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-k} P_{j}=1-P_{n-k+1} \geq \gamma
$$

and

$$
P_{j}=\frac{\pi_{j}}{\sum_{i=0}^{n-k+1} \pi_{i}} \quad \text { and } \quad \pi_{i}=(k \lambda / \mu)^{i}, \quad i=0, \ldots, n-k+1
$$

Asked is the smallest integer $n$ which satisfies Eq. (4.24) for given (fixed) $\gamma, k$, $\lambda$, and $\mu$. Often $n=k+1$ (one spare part) or $n=k+2$ (two spare parts) will be sufficient. In these cases, results of Table 6.8 (or Eq. (6.140)) with $v_{i}=k \lambda$ yield

$$
\begin{aligned}

Maintenance strategies can be very different according to the objective to be reached (type of maintenance policies, minimization of system down time or spare parts, availability maximization by given cost and / or logistic support, etc.). Among possible maintenance strategies [2.34, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2, 4.6, 4.8, 4.14, 4.18, 4.30, 6.3, A7.4(1962)], this section unifies and extends basic repair/replacement policies. Preliminary investigations on a new, approach for mission oriented high safety systems (Active System Control ASC, superimposing a periodic check to preventive maintenance) are introduced in [4.26], with practical realizations in [4.4], see also [5.77]. Cost aspects related to maintenance strategies and to spare parts provisioning are considered in this section and in Section 4.7. For undetected fault times one can refer to Eqs. (A6.30) and (6.223) for a practical application.

In the following it is assumed that the item considered is new at $t=0$, its failurefree time $\tau>0$ has distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x)$, density $\mathrm{f}(x)$, and finite mean $\mathrm{E}[\tau] \&$ variance $\operatorname{Var}[\tau]$. Furthermore, in Sections 4.6.1 \& 4.6.2, repairs/replacements are performed in a negligible time. Section 4.6.1 considers the case in which the item is as-good-as-new after each maintenance action, planned (preventive maintenance) or at failure (repair). In section 4.6.2, the item is as-good-as-new only after planned maintenance actions, but as-bad-as-old after repairs (minimal repair at failure). Considerations with finite repair/replacement times are in Sections 4.6.3 \& 6.8.2. ${ }^{+)}$

From the results of Sections 6.2-6.11, the following conclusions can be drawn:

1. As long as MTTR $<<$ MTTF holds for each element, shape of distribution functions of repair times has small influence on $M T T F_{S i} \& P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ (pp. 206-07).
2. As a consequence of Point 1 , it is preferable to start investigations by assuming Markov models (constant failure \& repair rates for all elements, Table 6.2); in a second step, more appropriate distribution functions can be considered (p. 277).
3. The assumption (6.2) of no further failure at system down has no influence on the reliability function; it support the existence of regeneration states (even better if also (6.3) holds, see p. 240) and allows a reduction of the state space.
4. Already for moderately large systems, use of Markov models can become timeconsuming (up to $e \cdot n$ ! states for a rel. block diagram with $n$ elements, p. 226); approximate expressions are thus important, and the macro-structures introduced in Section 6.7 (Table 6.10) adheres well to many practical applications.
5. For large systems or complex structures, following possibilities are available:

- work with a diagram of transition rates or a time schedule,
- calculate only the mean time to failure and steady-state availability at system level (Table 6.2, Eqs. (A7.126), (A7.173), (A7.131), (A7.178)),
- use approximate expressions (Sections 6.7 \& 6.9.7, Tables 6.9 \& 6.10),
- use alternative methods or Monte-Carlo simulation (Section 6.9).

Give the interval reliability $\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)$ for the case of a constant failure rate $\lambda \quad\left(\lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0}\right)$.

## Solution

With $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$ it follows that

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=e^{-\lambda(t+\theta)}+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{d u u}(x) e^{-\lambda(t+\theta-x)} d x=\left[e^{-\lambda t}+\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~h}_{d u u}(x) e^{-\lambda(t-x)} d x\right] e^{-\lambda \theta}
$$

Comparison with Eq. (6.17) for $\mathrm{F}(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x}$ yields

$$
\operatorname{IR}_{S 0}(t, t+\theta)=\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \cdot e^{-\lambda \theta}, \quad \text { for } \lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0}
$$

It must be pointed out that the product rule in Eq. 6.27, expressing $\operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ in $[t, t+\theta]$ | new at $t=0\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{u p$ at $t \mid$ new at $t=0\} \cdot \operatorname{Pr}\{$ no failure in $(t, t+\theta] \mid u p$ at $t\}$,
only holds because of const.failure rate $\lambda(x)=\lambda$ (memoryless property, p.458);
in the general case, the 2 nd term is $\operatorname{Pr}\{$ no failure in $(t, t+\theta] \mid$ (up at $t \cap$ new at $t=0)\}$, which differs from $\operatorname{Pr}\{$ no failure in $(t, t+\theta] \mid u p$ at $t\}$ for $\lambda(x) \neq \lambda$;
also should the use of $\operatorname{IR}\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right)$ as reliability $\mathrm{R}\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right)$, as in [A1.4], be dropped, to avoid misuses (see also remarks on pp. 40, 397, 442).# 6.2.1.5 Special Kinds of Availability 

In addition to the point and average availability (Sections 6.2.1.2 and 6.2.1.3), there are several other kinds of availability useful for practical applications [6.5 (1973)]:

1. Mission Availability: The mission availability $\mathrm{MA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, t_{o}\right)$ gives the probability that in a mission of total operating time (total up time) $T_{o}$ each failure can be repaired within a time span $t_{o}$, given item new at $t=0$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{MA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, t_{o}\right)= & \operatorname{Pr}\{\text { each individual failure occuring in a mission with total op- } \\
& \text { erating time } T_{o} \text { can be repaired in a time } \leq t_{o} \mid \text { new at } t=0\} \text {. }
\end{aligned}
$$

Mission availability is important in applications where interruptions of length $\leq t_{o}$ can be accepted. Its calculation considers all cases with $n=0,1, \ldots$ failures, taking care that at the end of the mission the item is operating (to reach the given (fixed) operating time $T_{o}$ ). Thus, for given (fixed) $T_{o}, t_{o}>0$

$$
\mathrm{MA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, t_{o}\right)=1-\mathrm{F}\left(T_{o}\right)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\mathrm{F}_{n}\left(T_{o}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{n+1}\left(T_{o}\right)\right)\left(\mathrm{G}\left(t_{o}\right)\right)^{n,+1}
$$

holds. $\mathrm{F}_{n}\left(T_{o}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{n+1}\left(T_{o}\right)$ is the probability for $n$ failures during the total operating time $T_{o}$ (Eq. (A7.14) with $\left.\mathrm{F}_{A}(x)=\mathrm{F}(x)\right) ;\left(\mathrm{G}\left(t_{o}\right)\right)^{n}$ is the probability that all $n$ repair times will be shorter than $t_{o}$. For constant failure rate $\lambda$ it holds that $\mathrm{F}_{n}\left(T_{o}\right)-\mathrm{F}_{n+1}\left(T_{o}\right)=\left(\lambda T_{o}\right)^{n} e^{-\lambda T_{o}} / n$ ! (Eq. (A7.41)) and thus

$$
\mathrm{MA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, t_{o}\right)=e^{-\lambda T_{o}\left(1-\mathrm{G}\left(t_{o}\right)\right)}, \quad \text { for } \lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0}
$$

2. Work-Mission Availability: The work-mission availability $\mathrm{WMA}_{S 0}\left(T_{o}, x\right)$ gives the probability that the sum of the repair times for all failures occurring in a mission of total operating time (total up time) $T_{o}$ is $\leq x$, given item new a $t=0$

$$

# Example 6.3 

Show that for a repairable one-item structure in continuous operation (Assumption (6.1)), the limit

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=P A_{S}=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}
$$

is valid for any distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x), \mathrm{F}_{A}(x), \mathrm{G}(x), \mathrm{G}_{A}(x)$ satisfying conditions (6.8) (6.12), and for which $\mathrm{f}(x), \mathrm{f}_{A}(x), \mathrm{g}(x), \mathrm{g}_{A}(x)$ go to 0 as $x \rightarrow \infty$.

## Solution

Using the renewal density theorem Eq. (A7.31), by considering Fig. A7.3 (p. 491), it follows that

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{~h}_{\text {duu }}(t)=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{~h}_{\text {dud }}(t)=\frac{1}{M T T F+M T T R}
$$

Furthermore, applying the key renewal theorem Eq.(A7.29) to $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$ given by Eq.(6.42) yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \mathrm{PA}_{S}(t) & =p\left(1-1+\frac{\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x}{M T T F+M T T R}\right)+(1-p) \frac{\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\mathrm{F}(x)) d x}{M T T F+M T T R} \\
& =p \frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}+(1-p) \frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}=\frac{M T T F}{M T T F+M T T R}
\end{aligned}
$$

The limits $1 /(M T T F+M T T R)$ and $M T T F /(M T T F+M T T R)$ can also be obtained from the final value theorem of the Laplace transform (Table A9.7a), considering for $s \rightarrow 0$

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\hat{\mathrm{f}}(s)=1-s M T T F+\mathrm{o}(s), & \hat{\mathrm{f}}_{A}(s)=1-s \mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{0}\right]+\mathrm{o}(s) \\
\hat{\mathrm{g}}(s)=1-s M T T R+\mathrm{o}(s), & \hat{\mathrm{g}}_{A}(s)=1-s \mathrm{E}\left[\tau_{0}^{\prime}\right]+\mathrm{o}(s)
\end{array}
$$

with $\mathrm{o}(s)$ as per Eq. (A7.89) and using Eq. (A7.50). When considering $\hat{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)$ for availability calculations, the approximation given by Eq. (6.54) often leads to $P A_{S}=1$, already by simple redundancy structures. In these cases, Eq. (6.113) has to be used.
Supplementary results: For $t \rightarrow \infty, 1 /(M T T F+M T T R)$ holds also for $h_{\text {udu }}(t), h_{\text {udd }}(t), h_{\text {ud }}(t)$ $=p h_{\text {udu }}(t)+(1-p) h_{\text {udd }}(t) \& h_{d u}(t)=p h_{\text {duu }}(t)+(1-p) h_{\text {dud }}(t)$ (see also Eqs. (A7.60) \& (A7.177)).

In the case of constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda(x)=\lambda \equiv \lambda_{S 0} \& \mu(x)=\mu \equiv \mu_{S}\right)$ Eq. (6.42) yields (Eq. (A7.50), Table A9.7b)

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)=\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}+\left(p-\frac{\mu}{\lambda+\mu}\right) e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t}=P A_{S}+\left(p-P A_{S}\right) e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t}
$$

Thus, for this important case, the convergence of $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t)$ toward $P A_{S}=\mu /(\lambda+\mu)$is exponential with a time constant $1 /(\lambda+\mu)<1 / \mu=M T T R$. In particular, for $p=1$, i. e. for $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(0)=1$ and $\mathrm{PA}_{S}(t) \equiv \mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$, it follows that

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)-P A_{S}=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu} e^{-(\lambda+\mu) t} \leq \frac{\lambda}{\mu} e^{-\mu t}=\lambda M T T R e^{-t / M T T R}
$$

Generalizing the distribution function $\mathrm{G}(x)$ of the repair time and/or $\mathrm{F}(x)$ of the failure-free time, $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ can oscillate damped (as in general for the renewal density $\mathrm{h}(t)$ given by Eq. (A7.18)). However, for constant failure rate $\lambda$ and providing $\lambda M T T R$ sufficiently small and some rather weak conditions on the density $\mathrm{g}(x)$, lower and upper bounds on $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ can be found [6.25]

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \geq \frac{1}{1+\lambda M T T R}-c_{l} \frac{\lambda M T T R}{1+\lambda M T T R} e^{-(\lambda+1 / M T T R) t}, \quad t \geq 0
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \leq \frac{1}{1+\lambda M T T R}+c_{u} \frac{\lambda M T T R}{1+\lambda M T T R} e^{-(\lambda+1 / M T T R) t}, \quad t \geq 0
$$

$c_{l}=1$ holds for many practical applications ( $\lambda M T T R \ll 0.1$ ). Sufficient conditions for $c_{u}=1$ are given in [6.25]. However, conditions on $c_{u}$ are less important as on $c_{l}$, since $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t) \leq 1$ is always true. The case of a gamma distribution with density $\mathrm{g}(x)=\alpha^{\beta} x^{\beta-1} e^{-\alpha x} / \Gamma(\beta)$, mean $\beta / \alpha$, and shape parameter $\beta \geq 3$, leads, for instance, to $\left|\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)-P A_{S}\right| \leq \lambda M T T R e^{-t / M T T R}$ at least for $t \geq 3 M T T R=3 \beta / \alpha\right.$.

Generalization of the repair time distribution functions $\mathrm{G}_{i}(x)$, with densities $\mathrm{g}_{i}(x)$ and $\mathrm{G}_{i}(0)=0$, leads to a semi-Markov process (see pp. 521 - 22) with state space $Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{n}$, as in Fig. 6.5; this because of Assumption (6.2) of no further failures at system down (implying also (6.3) of only one repair crew). The reliability function and the mean time to failure are still given by Eqs. (6.60) and (6.61). For the point availability let's first calculate the semi-Markov transition probabilities $\mathrm{Q}_{i j}(x)$ using Table 6.2

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Q}_{0 i}(x) & =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{0 i} \leq x \cap \tau_{0 k}>\tau_{0 i}, \quad k \neq i\right\} \\
& =\int_{0}^{x} \lambda_{i} e^{-\lambda_{i} y} \prod_{k \neq i} e^{-\lambda_{k} y} d y=\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\lambda_{S 0}}\left(1-e^{-\lambda_{S 0} x}\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n \\
\mathrm{Q}_{i 0}(x) & =\mathrm{G}_{i}(x), \quad i=1, \ldots, n
\end{aligned}
$$

The system of integral Equations for the transition probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t)$ follows then from Table 6.2

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}_{00}(t)=e^{-\lambda_{S 0} t}+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \int_{0}^{t} \lambda_{i} e^{-\lambda_{S 0} x} \mathrm{P}_{i 0}(t-x) d x \\
& \mathrm{P}_{i 0}(t)=\int_{0}^{t} \mathrm{~g}_{i}(x) \mathrm{P}_{00}(t-x) d x, \quad i=1, \ldots, n
\end{aligned}
$$

For the Laplace transform of the point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)=\mathrm{P}_{00}(t)$ one obtains finally, from Eq. (6.69),

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{PA}}_{S 0}(s)=\tilde{\mathrm{P}}_{00}(s)=\frac{1}{s+\lambda_{S 0}-\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i} \tilde{\mathrm{~g}}_{i}(s)}=\frac{1}{s+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i}\left(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}_{i}(s)\right)}
$$

from which, the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point and average availability

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_{i} M T T R_{i}}
$$

obtained using $\lim _{s \rightarrow 0}(1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(s))=s \cdot M T T R$, as per Eq. (6.54), and (Eq. (A6.38))

$$
M T T R_{i}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(1-\mathrm{G}_{i}(x)\right) d x

# Example 6.6 

Give the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point availability $P A_{S}$ for a 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with two different elements $E_{1} \& E_{2}$, constant failure and repair rates $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \mu_{1}, \mu_{2}$ (one repair crew, ideal failure detection \& switch).

## Solution

Figure 6.9 gives the reliability block diagram and the diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t] . \quad M T T F_{S 0}$ and $P A_{S}$ can be calculated from appropriate systems of algebraic equations. According to Table 6.2 and considering Fig. 6.9 it follows for the mean time to failure that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M T T F_{S 0}=\left(1+\lambda_{1} M T T F_{S 1}+\lambda_{2} M T T F_{S 2}\right) /\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) \\
& M T T F_{S 1}=\left(1+\mu_{1} M T T F_{S 0}\right) /\left(\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}\right), \quad M T T F_{S 2}=\left(1+\mu_{2} M T T F_{S 0}\right) /\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

which leads to

$$
M T T F_{S 0}=\frac{\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)\left(\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}\right)+\lambda_{1}\left(\lambda_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)+\lambda_{2}\left(\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}\right)}{\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)}
$$

and in particular for $\lambda_{1} \ll \mu_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2} \ll \mu_{2}$,

$$
M T T F_{S 0} \approx \mu_{1} \mu_{2} /\left(\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)\right)
$$

As for Eq. (6.93), the reliability function can be expressed by

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t) \approx e^{-\lambda_{S 0} t} \quad \text { with } \quad \lambda_{S 0} \equiv \frac{1}{M T T F_{S 0}} \approx \frac{\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)}{\mu_{1} \mu_{2}}=\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_{1}}+\frac{1}{\mu_{2}}\right)
$$

$\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=\lambda \& \mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\mu$ yield results as per Table 6.6 (for active redundancy). For the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point availability and average availability, $P A_{S}=A A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{2}$ holds with $P_{0}, P_{1}$, and $P_{2}$ as solution of (Table 6.2)

Figure 6.9 Reliability block diagram and diagram of the transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t]$ for a repairable 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with two different elements, constant failure \& repair rates $\left(\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \mu_{1}, \mu_{2}\right)$, ideal failure detection \& switch, one repair crew with repair as per first-in first-out ( $Z_{3} \& Z_{4}$ down states (absorbing for reliability calculation), arbitrary $t, \delta t \downarrow 0$, Markov process; see Fig. A7.4 on p. 504 for further possibilities)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) P_{0}=\mu_{1} P_{1}+\mu_{2} P_{2}, \quad\left(\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}\right) P_{1}=\lambda_{1} P_{0}+\mu_{2} P_{4} \\
& \left(\lambda_{1}+\mu_{2}\right) P_{2}=\lambda_{2} P_{0}+\mu_{1} P_{3}, \quad \mu_{1} P_{3}=\lambda_{2} P_{1}, \quad \mu_{2} P_{4}=\lambda_{1} P_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

One (arbitrarily chosen) of the five equations must be dropped and replaced by $P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{2}+P_{3}+P_{4}=1$. The solution yields $P_{0}$ through $P_{4}$, from which

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=P_{0}+P_{1}+P_{2}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{\lambda_{1} \lambda_{2}\left[\mu_{1}^{2}+\mu_{2}^{2}+\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)\left(\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)\right]}{\mu_{1} \mu_{2}\left[\mu_{1} \mu_{2}+\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right)\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}\right)\right]}}
$$

yielding, for $\lambda_{1} \ll \mu_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2} \ll \mu_{2}$,

$$
P A_{S}=A A_{S}=1-\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\mu_{1}} \cdot \frac{\lambda_{2}}{\mu_{2}} \cdot\left(\frac{\mu_{1}}{\mu_{2}}+\frac{\mu_{2}}{\mu_{1}}\right)
$$

$\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=\lambda \& \mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\mu$ yield results as per Table 6.6 (for active redundancy).

## Example 6.9

In a 1-out-of-2 warm redundancy with $E_{1}=E_{2}=E$ let the failure rates in the operating and reserve state be constant ( $\lambda$ and $\lambda_{r}$ ). For the repair time let us assume that it is distributed according to $\mathrm{G}(x)=1-e^{-\mu^{\prime}(x-\psi)}$ for $x>\psi$ and $\mathrm{G}(x)=0$ for $x \leq \psi$, with $M T T R \equiv 1 / \mu>\psi$. Assuming $\lambda \psi \ll 1$, investigate the influence of $\psi$ on the mean time to failure $M T T R_{S 0}$ and on the asymptotic \& steady-state value of the point availability $P A_{S}$.

## Solution

With

$$
\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\int_{\psi}^{\infty} \mu^{\prime} e^{-\mu^{\prime}(t-\psi)-\lambda t} d t=\frac{\mu^{\prime}}{\lambda+\mu^{\prime}} e^{-\lambda \psi}=\frac{\mu^{\prime}}{\lambda+\mu^{\prime}}(1-\lambda \psi)
$$

and considering $M T T R=\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mathrm{~g}(x) d x=\int_{\psi}^{\infty} x \mu^{\prime} e^{-\mu^{\prime}(x-\psi)} d x=\psi+\frac{1}{\mu^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{\mu}$; i. e. $\mu^{\prime}=\mu /(1-\mu \psi)$ and thus $\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\mu(1-\lambda \psi)^{\prime} /(\lambda+\mu(1-\lambda \psi))$, Eq. (6.108) and Eq. (6.110) lead to the approximate expressions

$$
M T T F_{S 0, \psi>0}=\frac{2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)}
$$

and

$$
P A_{S, \psi>0}=\frac{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)\right)}{\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)\left(\lambda+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)\right)+\mu^{2}(1-\lambda \psi)}=1-\frac{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)(1-\mu \psi))}{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu(1-\lambda \psi)\right)}
$$

On the other hand, $\psi=0$ leads to $1-\tilde{\mathrm{g}}(\lambda)=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$ and thus (Eqs. (6.92) and (6.87))

$$
M T T F_{S 0, \psi=0}=\frac{2 \lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu}{\lambda\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)} \quad \text { and } \quad P A_{S, \psi=0}=\frac{\mu\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}+\mu\right)}{(\lambda+\mu)\left(\lambda+\lambda_{r}\right)+\mu^{2}}
$$

Assuming $\mu \gg \lambda, \lambda_{r}$, yields (considering $\lambda \psi<\lambda / \mu<<1$ )

$$
\frac{M T T F_{S 0, \psi>0}}{M T T F_{S 0, \psi=0}}=1-\lambda \psi \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{P A_{S, \psi>0}}{P A_{S, \psi=0}}=1+\lambda \psi \frac{\lambda+\lambda_{r}}{\mu}=1
$$Equation (6.115) allows the conclusion to be made that,
for $\lambda$ MTTR $<<1$, the shape of the distribution function of the repair time has (for unchanged MTTR) a small influence on results at system level, in particular on the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0}$ and on the asymptotic \& steady-state point and average availability $P A_{S}=A A_{S}$ of a 1-out-of-2 redundancy.

Above conclusion can often be extended to more complex structures. Example 6.10 shows a numerical comparison for the case of a 1-out-of-2 parallel redundancy.

# 6.5 $k$-out-of- $n$ Redundancy (Warm, Identical Elements, one Repair Crew) 

A $k$-out-of-n redundancy, also known as $k$-out-of-n: $G$, consists of $n$ often identical elements, of which $k$ are necessary for the required function and $n-k$ are in reserve state, when not under repair or waiting for repair. Assuming ideal failure detection and switching, the reliability block diagram is as given in Fig. 6.12. Investigations in this Section assume identical elements $E_{1}=E_{2}=\ldots .=E_{n}=E$, only one repair crew,

Figure 6.12 $k$-out-of- $n$ redundancy reliability block diagram (ideal failure detection \& switch)
and no further failures at system down (failures during repair at system level are not considered, as per assumption (6.2)). Section 6.5 .1 considers the case of warm redundancy with constant failure rate $\lambda$ in operation state, $\lambda_{r}<\lambda$ in reserve state, and constant repair rate $\mu$ (active redundancy for $\lambda_{r}=\lambda$, standby for $\lambda_{r} \equiv 0$ ). An extension to cover other situations in which the failure rate is modified at state changes (e. g. for load sharing) is possible using equations for the birth and death process developed in Appendix A7.5.5 (see also pp. 61-62). Section 6.5.2 investigates a 2-out-of-3 active redundancy with constant failure rate, arbitrary repair rate, one repair crew, and no further failures at system down, opening the way to general $n-k=1$ cases (Fig A7.11 on p. 527). Reliability and availability for $n-k=2$ are considered on pp. 528-29. The influence of a series element, imperfect switching, incomplete coverage \& common cause failures are investigated in Sections 6.6-6.8.

# 6.5.1 k-out-of-n Redundancy with Const. Failure \& Repair Rates 

Assuming constant failure and repair rates, the time behavior of the $k$-out-of- $n$ redundancy with identical elements can be investigated using a birth and death process (Appendix A7.5.5). Figure 6.13 gives the corresponding diagram of transition probabilities in $(t, t+\delta t\}$. From Fig. 6.13 and Table 6.2, the following system of differential equations can be established for the state probabilities $\mathrm{P}_{j}(t)=$ $\operatorname{Pr}\{$ in state $Z_{j}$ at $t\}$ of a $k$-out-of- $n$ warm redundancy with one repair crew and no further failures at system down (constant failure rates $\lambda \& \lambda_{r}$ and repair rate $\mu$ )

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{0}(t)=-\nu_{0} \mathrm{P}_{0}(t)+\mu \mathrm{P}_{1}(t) & \\
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{j}(t)=\nu_{j-1} \mathrm{P}_{j-1}(t)-\left(\nu_{j}+\mu\right) \mathrm{P}_{j}(t)+\mu \mathrm{P}_{j+1}(t), & j=1, \ldots, n-k \\
\dot{\mathrm{P}}_{n-k+1}(t)=\nu_{n-k} \mathrm{P}_{n-k}(t)-\mu \mathrm{P}_{n-k+1}(t)
\end{array}
$$

with

$$
v_{j}=k \lambda+(n-k-j) \lambda_{r}, \quad j=0, \ldots, n-k
$$

Assume a nonrepairable (up to system failure) 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with two identical elements with constant failure rate $\lambda$. Give the mean time to failure $M T T F_{S 0_{P M}}$ by assuming a preventive maintenance with period $T_{P M} \ll 1 / \lambda$. The preventive maintenance is performed in a negligible time span and restores the 1-out-of-2 active redundancy to as-good-as-new.

## Solution

For a nonrepairable (up to system failure) 1-out-of-2 active redundancy with two identical elements with constant failure rate $\lambda$, the reliability function is given by Eq. (2.22)

$$
\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)=2 e^{-\lambda t}-e^{-2 \lambda t}
$$

with time dependent failure rate $\lambda_{S 0}(t)=2 \lambda\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right) /\left(2-e^{-\lambda t}\right)$ as per Eqs. (2.10), (2.22). The mean time to failure with preventive maintenance follows from Eq. (6.194) as

Incomplete faults (failures \& defects) coverage occurs because of lack or failure in the fault detection and /or localization (pp. 113 \& 116). Fault coverage is defined as the proportion of faults that can be detected and localized under given conditions. ${ }^{+)}$ It applies in particular to redundant structures. A fault coverage greater as 0.95 is often required for complex equipment. Lacks in the detection and/or localization lead to hidden faults, often not covered by automatic or semi-automatic diagnosis, and thus localizable only at a repair or preventive maintenance. Hidden faults
can cause a serious reduction of the advantage given by a redundancy,
see e.g. Eqs. (6.220) \& (6.222) or (6.228) \& (6.229)). A binary decision diagram (BDD) is a directed acyclic graph obtained by successive Shannon decomposition (Eq. (2.38)) of a Boolean function. It applies in particular to the structure functions developed in Section 2.3.4 for coherent systems, using minimal path or cut sets. This allows for easy calculation of the reliability function $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ for the nonrepairable case (Eqs. (2.45), (2.47)) or point availability $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ for repairable totally independent elements (Eqs. (2.45), (2.48)). Frequently, BDDs are used to calculate $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$ or $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ for systems completely described by a fault tree with corresponding fault tree structure function $\phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right) . \quad \phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right)$ follows from a fault tree, see e.g. Figs. $6.41 \& 6.42$, or from the corresponding reliability block diagram, considering " 0 " for operating (up) and " 1 " for failure (down).

In relation to fault trees, a BDD is created starting from the top event, i. e. from $\phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right)$, down to the sink boxes using the Shannon decomposition (Eq. (2.38)) of the fault tree structure function at the node considered. Each node refers to a variable of $\phi_{F T}\left(\zeta_{1}, \ldots, \zeta_{n}\right)$ and has 2 outgoing edges, 0 -edge for operating and 1-edge for failure. Input to a node can be one or more outgoing edges from other nodes. The BDD terminates in 2 sink boxes labeled 0 for operating (up), 1 for failure (down). Indication 0 or 1 and an arrow help to identify the outgoing edge. Figure 6.41 gives two basic reliability block diagrams with corresponding fault trees, $\phi_{F T}$, and BDDs;
to obtain $\mathrm{R}_{S 0}(t)$, one moves from the top of the BDD following all possible paths down to the sink box " 0 ", taking in a multiplicative way $\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)$ or $\widetilde{\mathrm{R}}_{i}(t)=1-\mathrm{R}_{i}(t)$ according to the value 0 or 1 assumed by the variable $\zeta_{i}$ involved (similar is for $\widetilde{\mathrm{R}}_{S 0}(t)$; for $\mathrm{PA}_{S 0}(t)$ consider Eq. (2.48)).

### 7.1.2 Simple Two-sided Sampling Plans for the Demonstration of a Defective Probability $p$

In the context of an acceptance test, demonstration of a defective probability $p$ is often required, instead of its estimation (Section 7.1.1). The main concern of this test is to check a zero hypothesis $H_{0}: p<p_{0}$ against an alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: p>p_{1}$ on the basis of the following agreement between producer and consumer, the lot should be accepted with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\alpha$ if the true (unknown) defective probability $p$ is lower than $p_{0}$, but rejected with a probability nearly equal to (but not less than) $1-\beta$ if $p$ is greater than $p_{1}\left(p_{0}, p_{1}>p_{0}\right.$, and $0<\alpha<1-\beta<1$ are given (fixed) values).$p_{0}$ is the specified defective probability and $p_{1}$ is the maximum acceptable defective probability. $\alpha$ is the allowed producer's risk (type I error), i. e. the probability of rejecting a true hypothesis $H_{0}: p<p_{0} . \beta$ is the allowed consumer's risk (type II error), i. e. the probability of accepting the hypothesis $H_{0}: p<p_{0}$ when the alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: p>p_{1}$ is true. Verification of the agreement stated above is a problem of statistical hypothesis testing (Appendix A8.3) and can be performed, for instance, with a simple two-sided sampling plan or a sequential test. Availability estimation and demonstration for a repairable item in continuous operation could be based on results of Section 6.2 for the one-item repairable structure. Point estimate (with corresponding mean and variance) for the availability can be found for arbitrary distributions of failure-free and repair times (Section 7.2.2.3). However, interval estimation and demonstration tests can lead to some difficulties.

An unified approach for point \& interval estimation as well as for demonstration of the asymptotic and steady-state point and average availability $P A=A A$ for a repairable item in continuous operation with exponentially or Erlangian distributed failure-free and / or repair times is introduced in Appendices A8.2.2.4\& A8.3.1.4. Sections 7.2.2.1 and 7.2.2.2 deal with this approach. The case of exponentially distributed failure-free \& repair times, i. e. constant failure \& repair rates $(\lambda(x)=\lambda \&$ $\mu(x)=\mu)$ is considered in detail, extension to Erlangian distributions is given.

For constant failure \& repair rates $\lambda \& \mu$, the point unavailability $1-\operatorname{PA}(t)$ converge rapidly and exponentially with time constant $\approx 1 / \mu$ to the asymptotic \& steady-state value (similar for $1-\mathrm{AA}(t)$, Table 6.3)

$$
\widehat{P A}=1-P A=1-A A=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)=(\lambda / \mu) /(1+\lambda / \mu) \leqq \lambda / \mu
$$

To simplify considerations, it is assumed that the observed time interval $(0, t]$ is $>>1 / \mu$, terminates at the conclusion of a repair, and exactly $k$ (or $n$ ) failure-free times $\tau_{i}$ and repair times $\tau_{i}^{\prime}$ have occurred. Furthermore, considering $\lambda \ll \mu$,

$$
\widehat{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu
$$

is estimated instead of $\widehat{P A}=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)\left(\widehat{P A}_{a}-(\lambda / \mu)^{2}<\widehat{P A}<\widehat{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu\right) . \lambda / \mu$ is a probabilistic value of the asymptotic \& steady-state unavailability and has his statistical counterpart in $D T / U T$, where $D T$ and $U T$ are the observed down and up times. The procedures developed in Appendices A8.2.2.4 and A8.3.1.4 are based on the fact that the quantity $\mu \cdot D T / \lambda \cdot U T$ has a Fisher distribution with $v_{1}=v_{2}=2 k$ (or $2 n$ ) degrees of freedom. Section 7.2.2.1 deals with estimation of $\widehat{P A}_{a}$, Section 7.2.2.2 with demonstration of $\widehat{P A}$. Alternative methods are discussed in Section 7.2.2.3.

### 7.2.2.1 Availability Estimation (Erlangian Failure-Free and/or Repair Times)

Having observed for an item as-good-as-new at $t=0$ and after each repair (Fig. 6.2), with constant failure\& repair rates $\lambda \& \mu$, an operating time $U T=t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}$ and a repair time $D T=t_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+t_{k}^{\prime}$, the maximum likelihood point estimate for $\widehat{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu$ is

$$
\widehat{P A}_{a}=(\lambda / \mu)=D T / U T=\left(t_{1}^{\prime}+\ldots+t_{k}^{\prime}\right) /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{k}\right)
$$

$D T / U T$ is biased, unbiased is $(1-1 / k) D T / U T, k>1$ (p.571). $\widehat{P A}_{a}=\lambda / \mu$ is an approximation for $\widehat{P A}=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$, good for practical applications (abs. error $\left\langle(\lambda / \mu)^{2}\right)$.

# Example 7.7 

An item with constant failure rate $\lambda$ operates first for a fixed time $T_{1}$ and then for a fixed time $T_{2}$. Repair times are neglected. Give the probability that $k$ failures will occur in $T=T_{1}+T_{2}$.

## Solution

The item's behavior within each of the time periods $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ can be described by a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\lambda$. From Eq. (A7.39) it follows that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{i \text { failures in the time period } T_{i} \mid \lambda\right\}=\frac{\left(\lambda T_{i}\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda T_{1}}
$$

and, because of the memoryless property of the homogeneous Poisson process

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{k \text { failures in } T=T_{1}+T_{2} \mid \lambda\right\} & =\sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{\left(\lambda T_{i}\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda T_{1}} \cdot \frac{\left(\lambda T_{2}\right)^{k-i}}{(k-i)!} e^{-\lambda T_{2}} \\
& =e^{-\lambda T} \lambda^{k} \sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{T_{i}^{i}}{i!} \cdot \frac{T_{2}^{k-i}}{(k-i)!}=\frac{(\lambda T)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\lambda T}
\end{aligned}
$$

The last part of Eq. (7.26) follows from the binomial expansion of $\left(T_{1}+T_{2}\right)^{k}$. Eq. (7.26) shows that for $\lambda$ constant, the cumulative operating time $T$ can be partitioned in an arbitrary way from failure-free times of statistically identical and independent items (see note to Table 7.3 for a rule).Supplementary result: The same procedure can be used to prove that the sum of two independent homogeneous Poisson processes with intensities $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ is a homogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}$; in fact,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{k \text { failures in }(0, T] \mid \lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}\right\} \\
& =\sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{\left(\lambda_{1} T\right)^{i}}{i!} e^{-\lambda_{1} T} \frac{\left(\lambda_{2} T\right)^{k-i}}{(k-i)!} e^{-\lambda_{2} T}=\frac{\left(\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) T\right)^{k}}{k!} e^{-\left(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}\right) T}
\end{aligned}
$$

This result can be extended to nonhomogeneous Poisson processes.

### 7.3.2 Demonstration of an MTTR

The demonstration of an MTTR (in an acceptance test) will be investigated here by assuming that the repair time $\tau^{\prime}$ is lognormally distributed with known $\sigma^{2}$ (method 1-A of MIL-HDBK-470 [7.23]). A rule is asked to test the null hypothesis $H_{0}: M T T R=M T T R_{0}$ against the alternative hypothesis $H_{1}: M T T R=M T T R_{1}$ for given type I error $\alpha$ and type II error $\beta$ (Appendix A8.3). The procedure (test plan) is as follows:

1. From $\alpha$ and $\beta(0<\alpha<1-\beta<1)$, determine the quantiles $t_{\beta}$ and $t_{1-\alpha}$ of the standard normal distribution (Table A9.1)

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{t_{\beta}} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x=\beta \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{t_{1}} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x=1-\alpha
$$

From $M T T R_{0}$ and $M T T R_{1}$, compute the sample size $n$ (next highest integer)

$$
n=\frac{\left(t_{1-\alpha} M T T R_{0}-t_{\beta} M T T R_{1}\right)^{2}}{\left(M T T R_{1}-M T T R_{0}\right)^{2}}\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right)
$$2. Perform $n$ independent repairs and record the observed repair times $t_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, t_{n}^{\prime}$ (representative sample of repair times).
3. Compute $\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]$ according to Eq. (7.39) and reject $H_{0}: M T T R=M T T R_{0}$ if

$$
\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]>c=M T T R_{0}\left(1+t_{1-\alpha} \sqrt{\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right) / n}\right)
$$

otherwise accept $H_{0}$.
The proof of the above rule implies a sample size $n>10$, so that the quantity $\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]$ can be assumed to have a normal distribution with mean MTTR and variance $\operatorname{Var}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] / n$ (Eqs. (A6.148), (A8.7), (A8.8)). Considering the type I and type II errors

$$
\alpha=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]>c \mid M T T R=M T T R_{0}\right\}, \quad \beta=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] \leq c \mid M T T R=M T T R_{1}\right\}
$$

and using Eqs. (A6.105) and (7.49), the relationship

$$
c=M T T R_{0}+t_{1-\alpha} \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{0}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] / n}=M T T R_{1}+t_{\beta} \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{1}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] / n}
$$

can be found, with $\operatorname{Var}_{i}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]$ for $M T T R=M T T R_{i}(i=0,1)$ according to Eq. (7.42) $\left(\operatorname{Var}_{i}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right]=\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right) M T T R_{i}^{2}, i=0,1\right)$. The sample size $n$ (Eq. (7.50)) follows then from Eq. (7.52). The right hand side of Eq. (7.51) is equal to the constant $c$ as per Eq. (7.52). The operating characteristic curve can be calculated from

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{\text { acceptance } \mid M T T R\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\hat{E}\left[\tau^{\prime}\right] \leq c \mid M T T R\right\}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{d} e^{-x^{2} / 2} d x
$$

with (Eqs. (A6.105), (7.42), (7.52))

$$
d=\frac{M T T R_{0}}{M T T R} t_{1-\alpha}-\left(1-\frac{M T T R_{0}}{M T T R}\right) \sqrt{n /\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right)}
$$

Considering $n /\left(e^{\sigma^{2}}-1\right)$ from Eq. (7.50), one recognizes that the operating characteristic curve is independent of $\sigma^{2}$ (rounding of $n$ neglected), see Example 7.12.

# 7.4 Accelerated Testing 

The failure rate $\lambda$ of electronic components lies typically between $10^{-10}$ and $10^{-7} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$, and that of assemblies in the range of $10^{-7}$ to $10^{-5} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}$. With such figures, cost and scheduling considerations demand the use of accelerated testing for $\lambda$ estimation and demonstration, in particular if reliable field data are not available. An
accelerated test is a test in which the applied stress is chosen to exceed that encountered in field operation, but still below the technological limits; this in order to shorten the time to failure of the item considered by avoiding an alteration of the involved failure mechanism (genuine acceleration).

In accelerated tests, failure mechanisms are assumed to be activated selectively by increased stress. The quantitative relationship between degree of activation and extent of stress, the acceleration factor $A$, is determined via specific tests. Generally,
it is assumed that the stress will not change the type of the failure-free time distribution function of the item under test, but only modify parameters; in the following, this hypothesis is assumed to be valid; however, its verification is mandatory before a statistical evaluation of data (see also p.102).

Many electronic component failure mechanisms are activated through a temperature increase. Calculating the acceleration factor $A$, the Arrhenius model can often be used over a reasonably large temperature range (about $0-150^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for ICs ). The Arrhenius model is based on the Arrhenius law [7.10,3.43], which states that the rate $v$ of a simple (first-order) chemical reaction depends on temperature $T$ as

$$
v=v_{0} e^{-E_{a} / k T}
$$

$E_{a}$ and $v_{0}$ are parameters, $k$ is the Boltzmann constant ( $k=8.6 \cdot 10^{-5} \mathrm{eV} / \mathrm{K}$ ), and $T$ the absolute temperature in Kelvin degrees. $E_{a}$ is the activation energy and is expressed in eV . Assuming that the event considered (for example the diffusion between two liquids) occurs when the chemical reaction has reached a given threshold, and the reaction time dependence is given by a function $\mathrm{r}(t)$, the relationship be

### 7.6.1 General considerations

In Sections 7.2 - 7.5, data were issued from a sample of a random variable $\tau$, i. e. they were $n$ independent realizations $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ of $\tau>0$ distributed according to (a postulated) $\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq t\}$, and belonging to one of the following situations:

1. Life times $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$ of $n$ statistically identical and independent items, all starting at $t=0$ when plotted on the time axis (Figs. 1.1, 7.12, 7.14, A8.1).
2. Failure-free times separating consecutive failure occurrences of a repairable item (system) with negligible repair times, repaired (restored) as a whole to as-good-as-new at each repair; i. e. statistically identical, independent interarrival times with common distribution function $\mathrm{F}(x)$, yielding a renewal process.
To this data structure belongs also the case considered in Example 7.19.
A basically different situation arises when the observations are arbitrary points on the time axis, i. e. a general point process. To distinguish this case, the involved random variables

re-free times (interarrival times, by negligible repair times) are neither independent nor equally distributed.

Except for very large systems, for which the flow of failures can converge to a homogeneous Poisson process (p. 537), the only situation which leads to independent and equally distributed interarrival times is that of case 2 above,
which requires constant failure rate for all elements to avoid restoration at each repair of all not failed elements with time dependent failure rate.

## A6.7 Multidimensional Random Variables, Conditional Distributions

Multidimensional random variables (random vectors) are often required in reliability and availability investigations of repairable systems. For random vectors, the outcome of an experiment is a point in the $n$-dimensional space $\mathcal{R}^{n}$. The probability space $\{\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \operatorname{Pr}\}$ introduced in Appendix A6.1 (pp. 429 - 30) becomes $\left[\mathcal{R}_{i}^{n}, \mathcal{B}_{i}^{n}, \operatorname{Pr}\right]$, where $\mathcal{B}^{n}$ is the smallest event field which contains all parallelepipeds $\left(a_{1}, b_{1}\right) \cdot \ldots \cdot\left(a_{n}, b_{n}\right]=\left\{\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right): t_{i} \in\left(a_{i}, b_{i}\right\}, i=1, \ldots, n\right\}$. Random vectors are designated by Greek letters with an arrow $\left(\vec{\tau}=\left(\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}\right), \vec{\xi}=\left(\xi_{1}, \ldots, \xi_{n}\right)\right.$, etc.). For each subset $A \subseteq \mathcal{B}^{n}$, the probabilities $\operatorname{Pr}\{A\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\vec{\tau} \in A\}$ define the distribution law of $\vec{\tau}$ ( $n$-dimensional distribution function, $n>1$ ). The function

$$
\mathrm{F}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{1} \leq t_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n} \leq t_{n}\right\}, \quad-\infty<\tau_{i}, t_{i}<\infty
$$

where

$$
\left\{\tau_{1} \leq t_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n} \leq t_{n}\right\} \equiv\left\{\left(\tau_{1} \leq t_{1}\right) \cap \ldots \cap\left(\tau_{n} \leq t_{n}\right)\right\}
$$

is the distribution function of the random vector $\vec{\tau}$, known as joint distribution function of $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n} . \mathrm{F}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)$ is:

- monotonically nondecreasing in each variable
- zero (in the limit) if at least one variable goes to $-\infty$
- one (in the limit) if all variables go to $\infty$
- continuous from the right in each variable
- such that the probabilities $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{a_{1}<\tau_{1} \leq b_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}<\tau_{n} \leq b_{n}\right\}$, calculated for arbitrary $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}, b_{1}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $a_{i}<b_{i}$, are not negative (see e.g. [A6.9]).It can be shown that each component $\tau_{i}$ of $\vec{\tau}=\left(\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}\right)$ is a random variable with distribution function

$$
\mathrm{F}_{i}\left(t_{i}\right)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{i} \leq t_{i}\right\}=\mathrm{F}\left(\infty, \ldots, \infty, t_{i}, \infty, \ldots, \infty\right), \quad \mathrm{F}_{i}(-\infty)=0, \mathrm{~F}_{i}(\infty)=1
$$

$\mathrm{F}_{i}\left(t_{i}\right)$ is called marginal distribution function.
Similarly as given by Eq.(A6.9) for events, the random variables $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$ of $\vec{\tau}$ are mutually (statistically, stochastically) independent, independent in this book (p.435), if and only if, for each $1<k \leq n$ and arbitrary $k$-tulpe $\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{k}\right) \in \mathcal{R}^{k}$,

$$
\mathrm{F}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{k}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{k} \mathrm{~F}_{i}\left(t_{i}\right)
$$

holds, see e. g. [A6.9]. In particular, for $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$ independent

$$
\mathrm{F}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{~F}_{i}\left(t_{i}\right), \quad\left(\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n} \text { independent }\right)
$$

is satisfied for arbitrary $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$.
The random vector $\vec{\tau}=\left(\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}\right)$ is absolutely continuous if a function $\mathrm{f}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) \geq 0$ exists such that for any $n$ and $n$-tulpe $t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}$

$$
\mathrm{F}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)=\int_{-\infty}^{t_{1}} \ldots \int_{-\infty}^{t_{n}} \mathrm{f}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) d x_{1} \ldots d x_{n}
$$

$\mathrm{f}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$ is the density of $\vec{\tau}$, known also as joint density of $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$, and satisfies the condition

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \ldots \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\right) d x_{1} \ldots d x_{n}=1
$$

For any subset $A \subseteq \mathcal{B}^{n}$, it follows that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\left(\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}\right) \in A\right\}=\int \underset{A}{\ldots} \int \mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right) d t_{1} \ldots d t_{n}
$$

The density of $\tau_{i}$ (marginal density) can be obtained from $\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)$ as

$$
\mathrm{f}_{i}\left(t_{i}\right)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \ldots \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right) d t_{1} \ldots d t_{i-1} d t_{i+1} \ldots d t_{n}
$$

If the random variables $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$ of $\vec{\tau}$ are independent (mutually, statistically, stochastically independent) and have densities $\mathrm{f}_{1}(x), \ldots, \mathrm{f}_{n}(x)$, the random vector $\vec{\tau}$ has density

$$
\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}, \ldots, t_{n}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{f}_{i}\left(t_{i}\right), \quad\left(\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n} \text { independent }\right)
$$For a two dimensional continuous random vector $\vec{\tau}=\left(\tau_{1}, \tau_{2}\right)$, the function

$$
\mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2} \mid t_{1}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right)}{\mathrm{f}_{1}\left(t_{1}\right)}
$$

is the conditional density of $\tau_{2}$ under the condition $\tau_{1}=t_{1}$, with $\mathrm{f}_{1}\left(t_{1}\right)>0$. Similarly, $\mathrm{f}_{1}\left(t_{1} \mid t_{2}\right)=\mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right) / \mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2}\right)$ is the conditional density for $\tau_{1}$ given $\tau_{2}=t_{2}$, with $\mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2}\right)>0$. For the marginal density of $\tau_{2}$ it follows that

$$
\mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2}\right)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}\left(t_{1}, t_{2}\right) d t_{1}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}_{1}\left(t_{1}\right) \mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2} \mid t_{1}\right) d t_{1}
$$

Therefore, for any $A \in \mathscr{B}^{2}$

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{2} \in A\right\}=\int_{A} \mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2}\right) d t_{2}=\int_{A}\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}_{1}\left(t_{1}\right) \mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2} \mid t_{1}\right) d t_{1}\right) d t_{2}
$$

and in particular

$$
\mathrm{F}_{2}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau_{2} \leq t\right\}=\int_{-\infty}^{t} \mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2}\right) d t_{2}=\int_{-\infty}^{t}\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}_{1}\left(t_{1}\right) \mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2} \mid t_{1}\right) d t_{1}\right) d t_{2}
$$

Equations (A6.58) \& (A6.59) lead to the Bayes theorem for continuous random variables

$$
\mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2} \mid t_{1}\right)=\left(\mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2}\right) \mathrm{f}_{1}\left(t_{1} \mid t_{2}\right)\right) / \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}_{2}\left(t_{2}\right) \mathrm{f}_{1}\left(t_{1} \mid t_{2}\right) d t_{2}
$$

used in Bayesian statistics.
Two dimensional distribution function, known as bivariate distributions, have been proposed for some reliability models, see e. g. [2.34 (1975)].

## A6.5 Random Variables, Distribution Functions

If the result of an experiment with a random outcome is a (real) number, then the underlying quantity is a (real) random variable. For instance, the number appearing when throwing a die is a random variable taking values in $\{1, \ldots, 6\}$, the life time of an item takes on values in $(0, \infty)$. Random variables are designated hereafter with Greek letters $\tau, \xi, \zeta$, etc. The triplet $[\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \operatorname{Pr}]$ introduced in Appendix A6.2 becomes $[\mathcal{R}, \mathcal{B}, \operatorname{Pr}]$, where $\mathcal{R}=(-\infty, \infty)$ and $\mathcal{B}$ is the smallest event field containing all (semi) intervals $(a, b]$ with $a<b$. The probabilities $\operatorname{Pr}\{A\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \in A\}, A \in \mathcal{B}$, define the distribution law of the random variable. Among the many possibilities to characterize this distribution law, the most frequently used is to define

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq t\}, \quad-\infty<\tau, t<\infty
$$

$\mathrm{F}(t)$ is called the (cumulative) distribution function of the random variable $\tau{ }^{+}$) For each $t, \mathrm{~F}(t)$ gives the probability that the random variable will assume a value smaller than or equal to $t$. Since $s>t$ implies $\{\tau \leq t\} \leq\{\tau \leq s\}, \mathrm{F}(t)$ is a nondecreasing function. Moreover, $\mathrm{F}(-\infty)=0$ and $\mathrm{F}(\infty)=1$. I $\mathrm{f} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau=t_{0}\right\}>0$ holds, then $\mathrm{F}(t)$ has a jump of height $\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau=t_{0}\right\}=\mathrm{F}\left(t_{0}\right)-\mathrm{F}\left(t_{0}-0\right)$ at $t_{0}$. As stated with Eq. (A6.19), $\mathrm{F}(t)$ is continuous from the right (Fig. A8.1); however, $\mathrm{F}(t)$ can have at most a countable number of jumps (see e.g. [A6.9]). The probability that the random variable $\tau$ takes on a value within the interval $(a, b]$ is (Fig. A6.2)

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{a<\tau \leq b\}=\mathrm{F}(b)-\mathrm{F}(a)
$$

1. Discrete random variables: A random variable $\tau$ is discrete if it can only assume a finite or countable number of values, i. e. if there is a sequence $t_{1}, t_{2}, \ldots$ such that

p_{k}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\tau=t_{k}\right\}, \quad \text { with } \quad \sum_{k} p_{k}=1

A discrete random variable is best described by a table

| Values of $\tau$ | $t_{1}$ | $t_{2}$ | $\ldots$ |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |

The distribution function $\mathrm{F}(t)$ of a discrete random variable $\tau$ is a step function

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)=\sum_{k: t_{k} \leq t} p_{k}
$$

Assuming the sequence $t_{1}, t_{2}, \ldots$ ordered $\left(t_{k}<t_{k+1}\right)$, then

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)=\sum_{j \leq k} p_{j}, \quad \text { for } \quad t_{k} \leq t<t_{k+1}, \quad\left(k=0,1,2, \ldots, t_{0}<t_{1}, p_{0}=0\right)

If only the value $k=1$ occurs in Eqs. (A6.21), $\tau$ is a constant $\left(\tau=t_{1}=C, p_{1}=1\right)$. A constant $C$ can thus be regarded as a random variable with distribution function

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { for } t<\mathrm{C} \\ 1 & \text { for } t \geq \mathrm{C}\end{cases}
$$

An important special case is that of arithmetic random variables. $\tau$ is arithmetic if it can take the values $\ldots,-\Delta t, 0, \Delta t, \ldots$, with probabilities

$$
p_{k}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau=k \Delta t\}, \quad k=\ldots,-1,0,1, \ldots
$$

2. Continuous random variables: The random variable $\tau$ is absolutely continuous if a function $\mathrm{f}(x) \geq 0$ exists such that

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\tau \leq t\}=\int_{-\infty}^{t} \mathrm{f}(x) d x
$$

$\mathrm{f}(t)$ is called (probability) density of the random variable $\tau$ and satisfies

$$
\mathrm{f}(t) \geq 0 \quad \text { and } \quad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{f}(t) d t=1
$$

$\mathrm{F}(t)$ and $\mathrm{f}(t)$ are related (almost everywhere) by (Fig. A6.2)

$$
\mathrm{f}(t)=d \mathrm{~F}(t) / d t
$$

Mixed distribution functions, exhibiting jumps and continuous growth, can occur in some applications, requiring a piecewise definition of the distribution function.

# A6.10.2 Weibull Distribution 

The Weibull distribution can be considered as a generalization of exponential distribution. A continuous positive random variable $\tau>0$ has a Weibull distribution if

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-(\lambda t)^{\beta}}, \quad t>0 ; \lambda, \beta>0 \quad(\mathrm{~F}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0)
$$

The density is given by

$$
\mathrm{f}(t)=\lambda \beta(\lambda t)^{\beta-1} e^{-(\lambda t)^{\beta}}, \quad t>0 ; \lambda, \beta>0 \quad(\mathrm{f}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0)
$$

and the failure rate (Eq. (A6.25)) by

$$
\lambda(t)=\beta \lambda(\lambda t)^{\beta-1}, \quad t>0 ; \lambda, \beta>0 \quad(\lambda(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq 0)
$$

$\lambda$ is the scale parameter $(\mathrm{F}(t)$ depends on $\lambda t)$ and $\beta$ the shape parameter. $\beta=1$ yields the exponential distribution. For $\beta>1$, the failure rate $\lambda(t)$ is strictly increasing ${ }^{*}$, with $\lambda(+0)=0 \& \lambda(\infty)=\infty$. For $\beta<1, \lambda(t)$ is strictly decreasing, with $\lambda(+0)=\infty$ and $\lambda(\infty)=0$. The mean \& variance are given by (Eqs.(A6.38), (A6.90), (A6.94) \& (A6.41), (A6.45), and Appendix A9.6 for $\Gamma(z+1)=z \Gamma(z)$ )

[^0]
