E[\tau]=\frac{\Gamma(1+1 / \beta)}{\lambda}=\frac{\Gamma(1 / \beta)}{\lambda \beta}
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\tau]=\frac{\Gamma(1+2 / \beta)-\Gamma^{2}(1+1 / \beta)}{\lambda^{2}}
$$

where

$$
\Gamma(z)=\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{z-1} e^{-x} d x, \quad z>0
$$

is the complete Gamma function (Appendix A9.6). The coefficient of variation (Eq. (A6.48)) $\kappa=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[\tau]} / E[\tau]$ is plotted in Fig. 4.5. For a given $E[\tau]$, the density of the Weibull distribution becomes peaked with increasing $\beta$. A simple analytical expression for the Laplace transform of the Weibull distribution function does not exist.

For a system without redundancy (series model) whose elements have independent failure-free times $\tau_{1}, \ldots, \tau_{n}$ distributed according to Eq. (A6.89), the reliability function is given by

$$
\mathrm{R}(t)=\left(e^{-(\lambda t)^{\beta}}\right)^{n}=e^{-\left(\lambda^{\prime} t\right)^{\beta}}, \quad t>0, \mathrm{R}(0)=1
$$

with $\lambda^{\prime}=\lambda^{\beta} \sqrt[n]{n}$ for $\lambda_{1}=\ldots=\lambda_{n}=\lambda$ or $\lambda^{\prime}=\sqrt{\beta / \lambda_{1}^{\beta}+\ldots+\lambda_{n}^{\beta}}$ for $\lambda_{1} \neq \ldots \neq \lambda_{n}$. Thus, the failure-free time of the system has a Weibull distribution with parameters $\lambda^{\prime}$ and $\beta$.

The Weibull distribution with $\beta>1$ often occurs in practical applications as a distribution of the failure-free time of components which are subject to wear-out and / or fatigue (lamps, relays, mechanical components, etc.). It was introduced by W. Weibull in 1951, related to investigations on fatigue in metals [A6.21]. B.W. Gnedenko showed that a Weibull distribution occurs as one of the extreme value distributions for the smallest of $n \rightarrow \infty$ independent random variables with the same distribution function (Weibull-Gnedenko distribution [A6.9, A6.10]).

For the Weibull distribution, notation with $\alpha=\lambda^{\beta}$ is often used. Also is the three parameters Weibull distribution known (see Example A6.14 and pp. 547-48)

$$
\mathrm{F}(t)=1-e^{-(\lambda(t-\psi))^{\beta}}, \quad t>\psi ; \lambda, \beta>0 \quad(\mathrm{~F}(t)=0 \text { for } t \leq \psi)
$$

## Solution

According to Eq. (A6.106) and the results of Appendix A6.9 (Eq. (A6.74)), the density of $\eta=\tau_{1}+\tau_{2}$ follows as

$$
\mathrm{f}_{\eta}(t)=\frac{1}{2 \pi \sigma_{1} \sigma_{2}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\left(\frac{\left(x-m_{1}\right)^{2}}{2 \sigma_{1}^{2}}+\frac{\left(t-x-m_{2}\right)^{2}}{2 \sigma_{2}^{2}}\right)} d x
$$

Setting $u=x-m_{1} \& v=t-m_{1}-m_{2}$, considering

$$
\frac{u^{2}}{\sigma_{1}^{2}}+\frac{(v-u)^{2}}{\sigma_{2}^{2}}=\left[\frac{u \sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}}}{\sigma_{1} \sigma_{2}}-\frac{v \sigma_{1}}{\sigma_{2} \sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}}}\right]^{2}+\frac{v^{2}}{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}}
$$

and setting finally $u \sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}} / \sigma_{1} \sigma_{2}-v \sigma_{1} / \sigma_{2} \sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}}=y$, the result

$$
\mathrm{f}_{\eta}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi} \sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}}} e^{-\frac{\left(t-m_{1}-m_{2}\right)^{2}}{2\left(\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}\right)}}
$$

is obtained. Thus the sum of two independent normally distributed random variables is also normally distributed with mean $m_{1}+m_{2}$ and variance $\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}$.
Supplementary results: If $\tau_{1}$ and $\tau_{2}$ are not independent, the distribution function of $\tau_{1}+\tau_{2}$ is a normal distribution with mean $m=m_{1}+m_{2}$ and variance $\sigma^{2}=\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}+2 \rho \sigma_{1} \sigma_{2}$, see e. g. [A6.9] ( $\rho=$ correlation coefficient as per Eq. (A6.67)).

The normal distribution often occurs in practical applications, also because the distribution function of the sum of a large number of independent random variables converges under weak conditions to a normal distribution (central limit theorem, Eq. (A6.148)).

Let $\delta_{1}, \delta_{2}, \ldots$ be a sequence of independent Bernoulli variables resulting from Bernoulli trials. The positive arithmetic random variable $\zeta$ defining the number of trials to the first occurrence of the event $A$ has a geometric distribution

$$
p_{k}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta=k\}=p(1-p)^{k-1}, \quad k=1,2, \ldots, \quad 0<p<1
$$

Equation (A6.131) follows from the definition of Bernoulli variables (Eq. (A6.115))

$$
p_{k}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta=k\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\delta_{1}=0 \cap \ldots \cap \delta_{k-1}=0 \cap \delta_{k}=1\right\}=(1-p)^{k-1} p
$$

The geometric distribution is the only discrete distribution which exhibits the memoryless property, as does the exponential distribution for the continuous case. In fact, considering $\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta>k\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\delta_{1}=0 \cap \ldots \cap \delta_{k}=0\right\}=(1-p)^{k}$ and that for any $k$ and $j>0 \operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta>k \cap \zeta>k+j\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta>k+j\}$, it follows that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta>k+j \mid \zeta>k\}=\frac{(1-p)^{k+j}}{(1-p)^{k}}=(1-p)^{j}=\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta>j\}
$$

From this, the failure rate $\lambda(k)$ (p.443) is time (step) independent and given by

$$
\lambda(k)=\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta=k \mid \zeta>k-1\}=\frac{p(1-p)^{k-1}}{(1-p)^{k-1}}=p, \quad k=1,2, \ldots, 0<p<1 .^{*}\}
$$

For the distribution function of the random variable $\zeta$ defined by Eq. (A6.131), it holds that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta \leq k\}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} p_{i}=1-\operatorname{Pr}\{\zeta>k\}=1-(1-p)^{k}, \quad k=1,2, \ldots, 0<p<1
$$

Mean and variance are (considering $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n x^{n}=x /(1-x)^{2}, \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n^{2} x^{n}=x(1+x) /(1-x)^{3}, x<1$ )

$$
\mathrm{E}[\zeta]=1 / p
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\zeta]=\frac{1-p}{p^{2}}
$$

The coefficient of variation (Eq. (A6.48)) is $\kappa=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}\{\tau\} / E[\tau]}=\sqrt{1-p}$.

For $n$ small, or $p(1-p)$ very small, the binomial distribution has to be used (Eqs. (A6.121), (A8.37), (A8.38)).# A7 Basic Stochastic - Processes Theory 

Stochastic processes are a powerful tool for investigating reliability, availability and safety of repairable equipment \& systems. A stochastic process can be considered as a family of time-dependent random variables or as a random function in time, and has thus a theoretical foundation based on probability theory (Appendix A6.7). The use of stochastic processes allows analysis of the influence of failure-free \& repair time distributions of elements, as well as of the system's structure \& characteristics, repair strategy and logistic support, on reliability, availability and safety of a given system. Considering applications given in Chapter 6, this appendix mainly deals with regenerative stochastic processes with a finite number of state, to which belong renewal, Markov, semi-Markov and semi-regenerative processes, including reward \& frequency/duration aspects. However, because of their importance in reliability investigations, some nonregenerative processes (in particular the nonhomogeneous Poisson process) are introduced in Appendix A7.8. This appendix is a careful introduction to stochastic processes, consistent from a mathematical point of view but still with reliability engineering applications in mind (demonstration of established theorems is referred, and for all other propositions or equations, sufficient details for complete demonstration are given). To simplify notation, mean is used for expected value \& independent for mutually (statistically, stochastically) independent. Selected examples illustrate the practical aspects.

Assuming $\operatorname{Pr}\{C\}>0$, prove that $\operatorname{Pr}\{(A \cap B) \mid C\}=\operatorname{Pr}\{B \mid C\} \operatorname{Pr}\{A \mid(B \cap C)\}$.
Solution
For $\operatorname{Pr}\{C\}>0$ it follows that

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\{(A \cap B) \mid C\}=\frac{\operatorname{Pr}\{A \cap B \cap C\}}{\operatorname{Pr}\{C\}}=\frac{\operatorname{Pr}\{B \cap C\} \operatorname{Pr}\{A \mid(B \cap C)\}}{\operatorname{Pr}\{C\}}=\operatorname{Pr}\{B \mid C\} \operatorname{Pr}\{A \mid(B \cap C)\}
$$

from which, considering the Markov property (Eqs. (A7.68)),

$$
\varphi_{i j}^{(2)}=\sum_{k=0}^{m} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+1}=Z_{k} \mid \xi_{n}=Z_{i}\right\} \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n+2}=Z_{j} \mid \xi_{n+1}=Z_{k}\right\}=\sum_{k=0}^{m} \varphi_{i k} \varphi_{k j}
$$

Results for $k>2$ follow by induction.
The transition probabilities $\varphi_{i j}$, together with the initial distribution

$$
A_{i}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{0}=Z_{i}\right\}, \quad i=0, \ldots, m, \sum A_{i}=1
$$

completely determine the distribution law of a Markov chain; in particular,

$$
\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{0}=Z_{i_{0}} \cap \xi_{1}=Z_{i_{1}} \cap \ldots \cap \xi_{n}=Z_{i_{n}}\right\}=A_{i_{0}} \varphi_{i_{0} i_{1}} \ldots \varphi_{i_{n-1} i_{n}}
$$

holds for arbitrary $i_{0}, \ldots, i_{n} \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$, and the state probability follows as

$$
\varphi_{j}(n)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n}=Z_{j}\right\}=\sum_{i=0}^{m} A_{i} \varphi_{i j}^{(n)}, \quad n=1,2, \ldots
$$

A Markov chain with transition probabilities $\varphi_{i j}$ is stationary (in steady-state) if the state probabilities $\varphi_{j}(n)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi_{n}=Z_{j}\right\}, j=0, \ldots, m$, are independent of $n$, i. e. if the initial distribution $A_{i}$ (Eq. (A7.72)) is a solution ( $\varphi_{j}$ ) of the system

$$
\varphi_{j}=\sum_{i=0}^{m} \varphi_{i} \varphi_{i j}, \quad \text { with } \varphi_{j} \geq 0 \text { and } \sum_{j=0}^{m} \varphi_{j}=1, \quad j=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

Furthermore, a Markov chain with a finite number of states $(m<\infty)$ is irreducible (irreducible and aperiodic, because of $m<\infty$ ) if every state can be reached from every other state, i. e. if for each $(i, j)$ there is an $n=n(i, j)$ such that

$$
\varphi_{i j}^{(n)}>0, \quad i, j \in\{0, \ldots, m\}, \quad n \geq 1
$$

It can be shown that the system (A7.74) possesses for $m<\infty$ a unique solution with

$$
\varphi_{j}>0 \quad \text { and } \quad \varphi_{0}+\varphi_{1}+\ldots+\varphi_{m}=1, \quad j=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

only if the Markov chain is irreducible (Markov theorem [A7.12], see e. g. also [A6.7 (Vol. I)]); in this case, the stationary distribution is also an ergodic distribution, i. e. $\varphi_{j}=\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \varphi_{i j}^{(n)}$. However, the system given by Eq. (A7.74)
must be solved by replacing one (freely chosen) equation by $\sum \varphi_{j}=1$.

A stochastic process $\xi(t)$ with state space $\left\{Z_{0}, \ldots, Z_{m}\right\}, 0<m<\infty$, is a Markov process in continuous time $(t \geq 0)$ with a finite number of states, if for $n=0,1,2, \ldots$, arbitrary time points $t_{n}+a>t_{n}>\ldots>t_{0} \geq 0$, and arbitrary $i, j, i_{0}, \ldots, i_{n} \in\{0, \ldots, m\}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi\left(t_{n}+a\right)=Z_{j} \mid\left(\xi\left(t_{n}\right)=Z_{i} \cap \xi\left(t_{n-1}\right)=Z_{i_{n-1}} \cap \ldots \cap \xi\left(t_{0}\right)=Z_{i_{0}}\right)\right\} \\
& =\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi\left(t_{n}+a\right)=Z_{j} \mid \xi\left(t_{n}\right)=Z_{i}\right\}=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t+a)=Z_{j} \mid \xi(t)=Z_{i}\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

holds. $\xi(t)(t \geq 0)$ is a jump function (jump process), as visualized in Fig. A7.10 on p. 522. The conditional state probabilities in Eq. (A7.77) are the transition probabilities of the Markov process and they will be designated by $\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t, t+a)$

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t, t+a)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(t+a)=Z_{j} \mid \xi(t)=Z_{i}\right\}, \quad t \geq 0, a>0
$$

Equations (A7.77) and (A7.78) give the probability that $\xi(t+a)$ will be $Z_{j}$ given that $\xi(t)$ was $Z_{i}$. Between $t$ and $t+a$ the Markov process can visit any other state (note that this is not the case in Eq. (A7.95), in which $Z_{j}$ is the next state visited after $Z_{i}$, as with Eq. (A7.158) for semi-Markov processes).

The Markov process is time-homogeneous if

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i j}(t, t+a)=\mathrm{P}_{i j}(a), \quad t \geq 0, a>0
$$

In the following only time-homogeneous Markov processes in continuous time $(t \geq 0)$ and with a finite number of states $(m+1)$ is considered. Equation (A7.79) expresses the memoryless property of the time-homogeneous Markov processes. $$

$$

and thus form a stochastic matrix. Together with the initial distribution

$$
\mathrm{P}_{i}(0)=\operatorname{Pr}\left\{\xi(0)=Z_{i}\right\}, \quad i=0, \ldots, m<\infty
$$

## A8.2.2.4 Availability Estimation (Erlangian Failure-Free and / or Repair Times)

Considerations of Section A8.2.2.3 can be extended to estimate the availability of a repairable item (described by the alternating renewal process of Fig. 6.2) for the case of Erlangian distributed failure-free and /or repair times (Appendix A6.10.3), and in particular for the case of constant failure and repair rates (Appendix A6.10.1).

Consider a repairable item in continuous operation, new at $t=0$ (Fig. 6.2), and assume constant failure and repair rates $\lambda(x)=\lambda, \mu(x)=\mu$ ( $x$ starting by 0 at the beginning of each operating or repair time, respectively). For this case, point and average unavailability rapidly converge (Table 6.3) to the asymptotic \& steady-state value $1-P A_{S}=1-A A_{S}=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$, given as $\overline{P A}=\overline{A A}$ to simplify the notation

$$
\overline{P A}=1-P \mathrm{~A}=1-A A=\overline{A A}=\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)
$$

$\lambda /(\lambda+\mu)$ is a probabilistic value and has his statistical counterpart in $D T /(U T+D T)$, where $D T$ is the down (repair) time and $U T=t-D T$ the up (operating) time observed in $(0, t]$. To simplify considerations, it will be assumed in the following $t \gg$ MTTR $=1 / \mu$ and that at the time point $t$ a repair is terminated and $k$ failure-free and repair times have occurred $(k=1,2, \ldots)$. Furthermore,

$$

## A8.3.3 Goodness-of-fit Tests for a Distribution $\mathbf{F}_{0}(t)$ with Unknown Parameters

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and the tests based on quadratic statistic can be used with some modification when the underlying distribution function $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t)$ is not completely known (unknown parameters). The distribution of the involved statistic $D_{n}, W_{n}^{2}, A_{n}^{2}$ must be calculated (often using Monte Carlo simulation) for each type of distribution and can depend on parameter values [A8.1]. For instance, in the case of an exponential distribution $\mathrm{F}_{0}(t, \lambda)=1-e^{-\lambda t}$ with parameter $\lambda$ estimated as per Eq. (A8.28) $\hat{\lambda}=n /\left(t_{1}+\ldots+t_{n}\right)$, the values of $y_{1-\alpha}$ for the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test have to be modified from those given in Table A8.1, e. g. from $y_{1-\alpha} \approx 1.36 / \sqrt{n}$ for $\alpha=0.05$ and $y_{1-\alpha} \approx 1.22 / \sqrt{n}$ for $\alpha=0.1$ to [A8.1]

$$
\alpha=0.05 \rightarrow y_{1-\alpha} \approx 1.09 / \sqrt{n} \quad \text { and } \quad \alpha=0.10 \rightarrow y_{1-\alpha} \approx 1.0 / \sqrt{n}
$$Also a modification of $D_{n}$ in $D_{n}^{\prime} \approx\left(D_{n}-0.2 / n\right)(1+0.26 / \sqrt{n}+0.5 / n)$ is recommended [A8.1]. A heuristic procedure is to use half of the sample (randomly selected) to estimate the parameters and continue with the whole sample and the basic procedure given in Appendix A8.3.2 [A8.11, A8.32].
